articles.author: Globe Newswire
articles.content: USA News Group News Commentary - Silver demand has outpaced supply every year since 2021, and the Silver Institute expects 2026 to make it six in a row. Much of the metal that answers that demand comes out of the ground alongside zinc, lead, copper and gold, which puts polymetallic deposits, where several payable metals share the same rock, close to the center of the silver supply story. In Canada’s Northwest Territories, new drilling at one of those deposits has just returned intervals grading more than 1,000 g/t silver equivalent within the footprint of a historic resource.

articles.content: New Express Entry points reward Canadian experience in high-wage jobs . For internationally trained professionals facing licensing barriers, that experience can be difficult to obtain. Consider two internationally educated nurses living in Canada. Both have years of clinical experience abroad and want to continue working in nursing. One has obtained Canadian registration and spent the past year as a registered nurse. The other has worked as a personal support worker while navigating licensing requirements. Under changes to Canada’s Express Entry system that recently took effect, their Canadian work histories can produce significantly different immigration scores. The difference is not necessarily their expertise, but their access to Canadian professional employment. This raises an important question: Is Canada selecting immigrants for the skills they possess or the opportunities they have already accessed? Read more: My grandfather kept his rejected degree for 50 years. Decades later, Canada still deskills immigrants What changed Express Entry ranks candidates for Canada’s main economic immigration programs using factors such as education, language proficiency and work experience. Candidates could already earn up to 80 points for Canadian work experience. Now, at least one year of Canadian experience in a high-wage occupation adds 20, 40 or 70 points, depending on the occupation’s median wage. A qualifying job offer can earn 50 to 100 points. Candidates receive whichever is higher, not both . The classification reflects an occupation’s typical earnings, not an individual’s salary. Eligible experience must generally be gained in Canada within the past 10 years in qualifying occupations. The federal government says the changes emphasize “factors linked to stronger economic outcomes.” . That rationale has merit. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada’s (IRCC) research on Express Entry labour-market outcomes found that immigrants with more Canadian work experience generally had higher employment incomes and wages after becoming permanent residents. But Canadian experience is not equally accessible to everyone. What the points actually measure In regulated professions, licensing bodies determine whether qualifications earned abroad meet Canadian standards. Assessments, examinations and supervised practice can delay professional entry, leaving qualified professionals working below their training level. Under the new system, that interim employment matters. Registered nurses qualify for an additional 40 points after a year of Canadian employment, while personal support workers are not on the high-wage list . Both occupations can count toward existing Canadian work-experience points, but only registered nurses receive the additional high-wage bonus. Experience gained abroad, however extensive, receives no equivalent high-wage bonus beyond existing skill-transferability points . The system therefore distinguishes workers partly by the occupations they can enter, reflecting both labour-market differences and potential barriers to professional recognition. What my research shows My research on Black internationally educated health professionals illustrates these barriers. In a mixed-methods study involving 132 participants in Canada and Nigeria, 65 per cent of respondents reported barriers to credential recognition . In a related study of Nigerian health workers in Canada, 76 per cent participated in activities to acquire new professional credentials . For many, obtaining Canadian professional recognition requires time and resources. During that transition, they may be unable to accumulate experience in the occupations the new points reward. A policy that rewards Canadian occupational experience also inherits the conditions that determine who gets that experience. Health-care recruitment difficulties Canada has prioritized health-care workers through dedicated Express Entry categories and, since December 2025, a category for doctors. Yet the doctors’ category requires Canadian work experience. This creates tensions between attracting internationally trained professionals and rewarding those who have already gained Canadian professional experience. The reforms don’t eliminate recognition of foreign experience. However, they give an additional advantage to candidates whose qualifications have already translated into qualifying Canadian employment. The professionals Canada seeks to attract may not always be those who benefit most from its new selection criteria. For a country facing health-care staffing pressures, the distinction matters: recruiting internationally trained professionals does not guarantee that their skills will be used in the occupations where they are needed. Read more: How the nursing shortage is affecting the health-care system, patients and nurses themselves What Canada should measure The changes may improve earnings among selected immigrants. But higher earnings alone doesn’t necessarily mean the system has identified the most capable professionals. It could also indicate that the system increasingly selects people who have already overcome barriers to higher-paying Canadian employment. IRCC should report invitation outcomes by occupation, particularly for regulated professions, and examine how internationally acquired qualifications influence selection outcomes. Closer co-ordination between federal immigration selection and provincial professional licensing could also identify where qualified candidates encounter barriers. Canada’s immigration system should recognize more than who has already succeeded in its labour market. It should also recognize the expertise internationally trained professionals bring with them. articles.content: Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette , the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters. These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies. The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront , increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people. Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed in the war — and potentially as many as 700,000 . For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it. The international dimension Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both prior to and after Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need. Providing aid to Ukraine has continued for the past four years, despite disruptions caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process. The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased domestic arms production , outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, air defence . Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies have and continue to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war has hit the Ukrainian economy , economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens. Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a rapid victory over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support. That support has taken many forms. Iran and North Korea have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers. Other countries, most notably China, have provided an economic lifeline to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians. Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials. Targeting support In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition , it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own. Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium . In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting. For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict. The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent . Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws . The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South. Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine . Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties. Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant. Read more: Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s removal of two top defence officials highlights the role of morale in long wars Attacking the secure ‘rear’ In military terms , the rear is the area furthest from the enemy and ideally secure from military threat. For both Ukraine and Russia, this area has been other countries. While Russia and Ukraine cannot attack the assets of other countries directly, they can and do engage in espionage against other countries. For Russia, these efforts have focused on destabilizing Europe using drones and other assets via attacks that that are easily deniable . Russia also seeks to create pressure through violating European air space . The more Russia destabilizes Europe, Ukraine’s primary ally, the better its chances in the conflict. For Ukraine, Russia’s aspirations to be a so-called Great Power mean its network is global — so Ukrainian special operation forces and intelligence agencies strike at Russian assets abroad where possible. These range from attacks in nearby areas, like the Baltics, to Africa and beyond. Read more: Putin wanted to make Russia great again. Instead, Ukraine is the new rising power in Europe While news agencies view this development as widening the conflict, and the United Nations may wish to prevent the conflict from going global, the reality is it’s been a global conflict since before 2022. The strikes in Libya and the Baltic, and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediate acknowledgement of Ukraine’s role, is just making it public. Iran and North Korea have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers. Other countries, most notably China, have provided an economic lifeline to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians. Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials. Targeting support In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition , it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own. Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium . In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting. For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict. The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent . Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws . The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South. Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine . Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties. Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant. Read more: Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s removal of two top defence officials highlights the role of morale in long wars Attacking the secure ‘rear’ In military terms , the rear is the area furthest from the enemy and ideally secure from military threat. For both Ukraine and Russia, this area has been other countries. While Russia and Ukraine cannot attack the assets of other countries directly, they can and do engage in espionage against other countries. For Russia, these efforts have focused on destabilizing Europe using drones and other assets via attacks that that are easily deniable . Russia also seeks to create pressure through violating European air space . The more Russia destabilizes Europe, Ukraine’s primary ally, the better its chances in the conflict. For Ukraine, Russia’s aspirations to be a so-called Great Power mean its network is global — so Ukrainian special operation forces and intelligence agencies strike at Russian assets abroad where possible. These range from attacks in nearby areas, like the Baltics, to Africa and beyond. Read more: Putin wanted to make Russia great again. Instead, Ukraine is the new rising power in Europe While news agencies view this development as widening the conflict, and the United Nations may wish to prevent the conflict from going global, the reality is it’s been a global conflict since before 2022. The strikes in Libya and the Baltic, and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediate acknowledgement of Ukraine’s role, is just making it public. articles.content: A television drama no longer needs a television-sized screen, or even a half-hour episode. Microdramas — serialized stories filmed vertically and delivered in episodes often lasting a minute or two — are becoming a growing part of the streaming business. The format first took off in China , where producers condensed familiar soap opera plots — such as secret fortunes, time travel and long-awaited revenge — into episodes short enough to watch while waiting for a bus. The total amount of users of microdrama apps in China grew from 10 million to 400 million in three years . Microdrama platforms have developed a distinctive business model that sets them apart from traditional TV. Viewers can watch a handful of episodes before having to purchase virtual coins, subscribe or watch advertisements to unlock more. On DramaBox, for instance, viewers of Think Again! I’m the Hidden Boss Mom can watch the first 16 episodes free before paying for the remaining 36. Read more: TikTok’s popular microdramas shrink TV into bite-sized chunks The model has helped create a fast-growing industry . Microdramas generated US$11 billion worldwide in 2025 and are estimated to earn about US$14 billion in 2026. But the industry’s growth does not guarantee profitability. Industry and market research shows that while production costs are lower, attracting audiences is expensive, competition is intensifying and regulation remains unpredictable. How microdramas find their audiences Microdramas primarily rely on two distribution strategies . The first uses short teaser clips on TikTok or Instagram to attract viewers to dedicated apps, such as ReelShort and DramaBox, where they then pay to watch complete series. The second strategy involves distributing entire series through established video platforms, such as YouTube, where advertising revenue can support production. Microdramas generated more than 6.5 billion views on YouTube in the first half of 2026 . YouTube has also introduced the ability to group shorts into seasons and episodes , making serialized viewing easier within the platform. Other companies are trying to capitalize on existing audiences. In October, Tencent introduced Green Bubble, a free microdrama service integrated into its WeChat app. Users can discover series through search, links in a channel’s video feed or a section highlighting what their friends are watching. TikTok has also announced a partnership with a studio to produce microdramas . Its parent company, ByteDance, also operates Hongguo, a short-drama application that relies on algorithm-driven recommendations to attract viewers. How the business model works Microdrama platforms use several approaches to generate revenue. On DramaBox, viewers can subscribe, buy coins to unlock episodes or earn coins by watching ads . Green Bubble is free to watch and generates revenue through advertisements inserted into episodes. The payment structure is central to the format. Unlike a cinema ticket that provides access to an entire film or a streaming subscription that unlocks a catalogue, microdrama apps can charge viewers at particular moments in a story , often at cliffhangers when they are asked to pay to find out what happens next. This approach has raised consumer protection concerns. The consumer protection committee in the Chinese province of Jiangsu recorded 167,870 online complaints and other consumer-related reports concerning microdramas in the first half of 2024. Complaints included unclear charging and refund policies, misleading payment arrangements and difficulties cancelling subscriptions. Its investigation also found that some platforms did not clearly disclose the total cost of watching a series. Older consumers were particularly vulnerable to repeated purchases . Some companies are starting to use microdramas as advertising vehicles. American food company Bob Evans, for example, is releasing a 20-episode holiday series Christmas at Maple Hollow Inn through its own channels. Microdrama studio Pixie Studios integrates the company’s products into the story . High revenue doesn’t mean bigger profits Despite the market’s growth, the economic longevity of the industry remains an issue. Attracting viewers can be expensive, even when producing the shows themselves costs relatively little. FlexTV’s parent company, Mega Matrix, reported that advertising expenses accounted for 43 per cent of its total revenue in the first half of 2026 . Crazy Maple Studio, which runs ReelShort, nearly doubled its revenue in 2025 to 5.72 billion yuan, while its company-wide net loss was about 86 million yuan . Production costs are comparatively low. American streaming company Mansa produces microdramas on budgets from US$100,000 to US$250,000 per series . Low production costs allow producers to experiment with new ideas and take risks that would be difficult to justify with traditional TV budgets. But they also lower the barrier of entry for competitors, making it easier for rival studios to produce similar content. A Wall Street Journal segment about the microdrama boom. Artificial intelligence could push production costs down further. Kunlun Tech, which owns DramaWave, estimates it can make a microdrama series with AI for under US$20,000 , compared with $150,000 to $200,000 for a comparable series with human actors in dominant markets. AI-generated productions are already making an impact, with more than 94 per cent of new microdramas in China this year being AI-generated . At the end of October, 86 of the 100 titles on Hongguo’s trending chart were reportedly AI-made . As AI-generated content becomes more common, demand for some human performers and production workers will likely decline . What may strain the business model Hollywood studios and video platforms are feeling the pressure, and established streaming services and social platforms are increasingly adopting elements of the format. Omdia found that microdrama apps generate more daily viewing time than the biggest streaming platforms . Disney+ has added a vertical clip feed , HBO Max has begun testing one and YouTube now encourages creators to publish vertical series . Competition from established platforms could give microdramas access to larger audiences, but it also puts pressure on dedicated apps to differentiate their content and retain subscribers. Regulation is another area of uncertainty, particularly in China. China’s broadcast regulator recently launched a two-month campaign targeting eight types of content, including violent, sexually suggestive and wealth-flaunting material . Platform content moderation is also being tested, as Hongguo faces a lawsuit over the alleged unauthorized use of actress Zhao Liying’s likeness in AI-generated microdramas . Other alleged victims have said they are preparing legal action , so more disputes may follow. Recent Chinese regulations on microdramas require platforms offering paid content to clearly disclose pricing information and prohibit the use of algorithms designed to encourage addictive behaviour or excessive spending. In the United States, California requires businesses to obtain express consent to automatic renewal and lets customers who sign up online cancel online . Though a cliffhanger can get someone to watch one more episode, the hard test will always come in the end. Will viewers open the app again on their own, or will the company have to place an advertisement to reach them again? articles.content: Recently, starting in August, poet and author Nayyirah Waheed began posting a series of images to Instagram that reignited existing debates within Instagram poetry. In her post, Waheed said Rupi Kaur’s bestselling book of poetry, milk and honey (2014), “extracted” the style, form and ideas of her 2013 self-published collection, salt . The author, based in the United States, also said that Andrews McMeel Publishing worked to erase Waheed from the narrative of Instapoetry, calling their actions “corporate gaslighting” and “hostile takeover attempts.” In 2018, Vice asked Kaur how she deals with accusations of plagiarism in general and those specifically by Waheed. She said that many other artists are looking at similar subjects and “me using a couple of words that the other person also uses, doesn’t equal plagiarism.” . One of the long-standing questions raised in this debate is who is the originator of Instapoetry? Did Kaur “extract” from Waheed as she says? And why did Kaur became the genre’s public face? The allegations of plagiarism from Waheed as well as her characterization of this process as anti-Black erasure are serious and warrant careful attention. Some reporters have also argued that the praise of Kaur’s poetry over Waheed’s is rooted in anti-Blackness . Waheed’s posts also make a broader challenge: that salt. didn’t just precede milk and honey , but established the visual and formal language later recognized as Instapoetry. Waheed self-published salt. in 2013 after gaining popularity on Twitter and Instagram, then self-published nemja in 2014. Kaur is considered one of the first and most successful Instapoets and has by and large become representative of the genre. Instapoetry is a genre of poetry that circulates on Instagram and often features short, free-verse lines, limited punctuation and line drawings. The poetry typically favours emotional directness, brevity and formal constraints, including lower-case typography and minimal punctuation . As a researcher studying women’s writing and publishing infrastructures, I argue that genres are formed through complex relations among communities, influences, audiences and platforms. Literary history often relies on the idea of one great individual who single-handedly creates a genre. But genres usually grow out of many writers, readers, influences and communities over time . Rupi Kaur, the face of Instapoetry Canadian poet Rupi Kaur, who also identifies as Punjabi Sikh, is arguably one of the most commercially successful Instapoets. Her poetry is often written in lower-case letters and sparingly includes punctuation. She says the style is one way to break English rules but it also reflects some of her heritage and the Gurmukhi script, which has no uppercase. . Kaur currently has more than four million followers on Instagram and has sold over 12 million books worldwide. She has said Instagram allowed her to sidestep gatekeepers to the publishing industry who were “never going to pay attention to (her) anyway.” Kaur’s success sparked heated debate in traditional poetry communities, with some arguing that Instagram democratized poetry by allowing previously marginalized writers to sidestep gatekeepers and publish outside traditional structures . Others, like British poet Rebecca Watts, characterize Instapoetry as “artless,” lament that poetry has not escaped “social media’s dumbing effect” and call Instapoetry a “huckster’s paradise.” Read more: Instapoetry is successful and there’s nothing wrong with that The ‘blueprint’ of a genre? Kaur self-published milk and honey in 2014. After Instagram censored her menstruation photographs , Kaur went viral and signed with Andrews McMeel Publishing who republished milk and honey to wide commercial success. In 2017, Rolling Stone dubbed her the “Queen of the Instapoets.” That same year, BookNet Canada named Kaur as a driving force behind increased poetry sales . In one of her September Instagram posts, Waheed says: “@rupikaur you took credit for my blueprint,” challenging the industry’s elevation of Kaur as the singular face of Instapoetry. By doing this, Waheed suggests that one person can be responsible for the founding of a literary style and history. But can any one writer supply the “blueprint” for an entire genre? Instapoetry’s influences As U.S.-based literary theorist Carolyn Miller explains in her foundational study on genre , genres are not formal categories but emerge through the ways we encounter, interpret, use and reproduce texts. Some of the text and style features Waheed says originated with her 2013 work, salt. , were not developed in isolation. They belong to a wider ecology of online writing and reading already taking shape across social media platforms throughout the 2000s-2010s, as I have argued in my PhD thesis. Several specific digital locations of this era can be seen as key influences to the later development of Instapoetry. From this perspective, lower-case typography, brevity, white space, illustration and emotional directness are formal conventions, not a genre in themselves. Tumblr, for example, was a particularly significant site of poetic experimentation for writers at this time. Its multimedia interface encouraged combinations of text, photographs, GIFs, drawings and handwritten fragments. Poetry circulated through tags such as #poetry, #poetsoftumblr and #spilledink, creating a participatory culture of reposting, remixing and response. Minimalist typography, including lower-case letters and sparse punctuation, was widespread on Tumblr as an internet vernacular rather than one writer’s signature. Digital spoken word communities, largely rooted in North American Black culture , also influenced the Instapoetry genre . By the 2010s, YouTube channels like Button Poetry had brought live poetry to large online audiences. These works favoured direct address, emotional intensity and accessible language, and often addressed gender, race, migration and trauma — themes that would become central to Instapoetry . Canadian Instapoets, including Kaur, were on Tumblr, performing at open mic nights in Toronto , Surrey and Delta, B.C. and watching slam performances on YouTube. These poets encountered — and were shaped by — poetry circulating through Tumblr, live readings and viral videos. The Instagram platform also played a critical role in developing the genre . The social media app was the first to focus predominantly on the visual , with images taking centre-stage and text — in the form of captions, comments and hashtags — framing the image. Instapoetry emerged through many writers, esthetics, technologies and audiences moving across platforms and between digital and in-person spaces. It became recognizable through self-publication, networked circulation, audience interaction, algorithms, performance, print and literary entrepreneurship. The genre can therefore be understood as something produced and continually negotiated by poets, readers, publishers, critics and platforms. Waheed has an important place in the genre’s history, but even an innovative writer cannot alone create a genre. Where do we go from here? Waheed’s recent posts reminds us that literary history is never neutral: it is shaped by who is remembered, who is marketed and whose innovations are made visible. Her allegations of the “extraction” of her work and her analysis that this is part of a continuum of anti-Black erasure require attention, particularly in an industry with long histories of marginalizing Black women writers. Waheed is an important and under-recognized figure in the genre, but Instapoetry has no sole architect. The history of Instapoetry is best understood as a story with more than one originator. It’s a history of overlapping influence, platform-specific experimentation, performance, readership and commercial power. The question then may be less “who owns Instapoetry?” than who’s been permitted to represent it — and who has profited from that representation. Kiera Obbard has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council Joseph-Armand Bombardier Canada Graduate Scholarship - Doctoral. She currently receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council as a Postdoctoral Fellow.

Others, like British poet Rebecca Watts, characterize Instapoetry as “artless,” lament that poetry has not escaped “social media’s dumbing effect” and call Instapoetry a “huckster’s paradise.” Read more: Instapoetry is successful and there’s nothing wrong with that The ‘blueprint’ of a genre? Kaur self-published milk and honey in 2014. After Instagram censored her menstruation photographs , Kaur went viral and signed with Andrews McMeel Publishing who republished milk and honey to wide commercial success. In 2017, Rolling Stone dubbed her the “Queen of the Instapoets.” That same year, BookNet Canada named Kaur as a driving force behind increased poetry sales . In one of her September Instagram posts, Waheed says: “@rupikaur you took credit for my blueprint,” challenging the industry’s elevation of Kaur as the singular face of Instapoetry. By doing this, Waheed suggests that one person can be responsible for the founding of a literary style and history. But can any one writer supply the “blueprint” for an entire genre? Instapoetry’s influences As U.S.-based literary theorist Carolyn Miller explains in her foundational study on genre , genres are not formal categories but emerge through the ways we encounter, interpret, use and reproduce texts. Some of the text and style features Waheed says originated with her 2013 work, salt. , were not developed in isolation. They belong to a wider ecology of online writing and reading already taking shape across social media platforms throughout the 2000s-2010s, as I have argued in my PhD thesis. Several specific digital locations of this era can be seen as key influences to the later development of Instapoetry. From this perspective, lower-case typography, brevity, white space, illustration and emotional directness are formal conventions, not a genre in themselves. Tumblr, for example, was a particularly significant site of poetic experimentation for writers at this time. Its multimedia interface encouraged combinations of text, photographs, GIFs, drawings and handwritten fragments. Poetry circulated through tags such as #poetry, #poetsoftumblr and #spilledink, creating a participatory culture of reposting, remixing and response. Minimalist typography, including lower-case letters and sparse punctuation, was widespread on Tumblr as an internet vernacular rather than one writer’s signature. Digital spoken word communities, largely rooted in North American Black culture , also influenced the Instapoetry genre . By the 2010s, YouTube channels like Button Poetry had brought live poetry to large online audiences. These works favoured direct address, emotional intensity and accessible language, and often addressed gender, race, migration and trauma — themes that would become central to Instapoetry . Canadian Instapoets, including Kaur, were on Tumblr, performing at open mic nights in Toronto , Surrey and Delta, B.C. and watching slam performances on YouTube. These poets encountered — and were shaped by — poetry circulating through Tumblr, live readings and viral videos. The Instagram platform also played a critical role in developing the genre . The social media app was the first to focus predominantly on the visual , with images taking centre-stage and text — in the form of captions, comments and hashtags — framing the image. Instapoetry emerged through many writers, esthetics, technologies and audiences moving across platforms and between digital and in-person spaces. It became recognizable through self-publication, networked circulation, audience interaction, algorithms, performance, print and literary entrepreneurship. The genre can therefore be understood as something produced and continually negotiated by poets, readers, publishers, critics and platforms. Waheed has an important place in the genre’s history, but even an innovative writer cannot alone create a genre. Where do we go from here? Waheed’s recent posts reminds us that literary history is never neutral: it is shaped by who is remembered, who is marketed and whose innovations are made visible. Her allegations of the “extraction” of her work and her analysis that this is part of a continuum of anti-Black erasure require attention, particularly in an industry with long histories of marginalizing Black women writers. Waheed is an important and under-recognized figure in the genre, but Instapoetry has no sole architect. The history of Instapoetry is best understood as a story with more than one originator. It’s a history of overlapping influence, platform-specific experimentation, performance, readership and commercial power. The question then may be less “who owns Instapoetry?” than who’s been permitted to represent it — and who has profited from that representation. She currently receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council as a Postdoctoral Fellow.
articles.title: What is Instagram poetry, and why are people arguing about who owns it?

articles.content: In the past six months, Canada has seen one weather extreme after another. Summer storms forced more than 50 Manitoba municipalities and First Nations to declare states of emergency. On July 1, up to 167 millimetres of rain fell on Ottawa . Wildfires also burned 4.5 million hectares of forest over the summer, and wildfire smoke left Toronto with some of the worst air quality in the world . Then came the strange autumn: the warmest in 80 years in eastern Canada, with 22 C highs in Ontario and Québec in November , Nunavut communities above freezing in November for the first time on record and atmospheric rivers that dumped more than 300 millimetres of rain on southern British Columbia . And on Nov. 11, 30 kilometres above the Arctic, came the latest shock: the earliest polar vortex breakdown ever recorded . Now, as December approaches, Canada faces two very different influences. A powerful El Niño generally favours milder winters, while a weakened polar vortex can sometimes bring Arctic cold farther south. Our analysis of 45 years of Canadian temperature data suggests that December could look very different across the country, with colder conditions more likely in much of western and central Canada and milder weather in parts of the north and east. A 68-year record broken The polar vortex is a ring of strong winds that circles the Arctic about 30 kilometres above the ground. These winds normally blow from west to east, helping keep very cold air near the pole. By mid-November, they usually reach about 100 kilometres per hour. But this year, the winds slowed, stopped and briefly reversed on Nov. 11. The cause was a rapid warming high above the Arctic, known as a sudden stratospheric warming . Large waves of air moving upward through the atmosphere can disturb the vortex, much like pushing a spinning top off balance. The previous record was Nov. 28, 1968. It tied the record on Nov. 28 last year. This year’s reversal lasted only about two days, and forecasts suggest the winds are recovering. Still, such an early reversal has never been seen in the 68 years it’s been recorded. The question now is whether this event will affect Canada’s weather in December. When the Arctic meets a super El Niño What happens high above the Arctic can sometimes affect the weather we feel on the ground. After a polar vortex disruption, changes can spread downward over the following two to six weeks . They can disturb the jet stream, the fast-moving winds that help guide weather systems. When the jet stream becomes more wavy, Arctic air can move farther south. This played a role in events such as the Texas freeze of 2021 and last January’s winter storm . But another major climate pattern is also at work. The Pacific Ocean is experiencing an exceptionally strong El Niño, which forecasters in the United States say could become one of the strongest on record . During strong El Niño winters, southern Canada often experiences milder-than-normal temperatures , particularly in western and central regions. A disrupted polar vortex can work in the opposite direction, increasing the chance of short periods of intense cold. Neither influence controls Canada’s weather on its own. What matters is how they interact and where their effects are strongest. What can Canadians expect this December? Our forecast points to clear differences across the country. British Columbia and Ontario each have a 72 per cent probability of a colder-than-normal December. Alberta and Saskatchewan also favour colder conditions, with probabilities of 71 and 68 per cent. Québec has a 68 per cent probability of milder weather. In Nunavut, that probability rises to 88 per cent. Yukon, meanwhile, has a 54 per cent probability of colder conditions, making its outlook much less certain. These percentages tell us how likely December is to be warmer or colder than normal, not how high or low temperatures will go. But there is something important that monthly averages cannot show. A warmer-than-normal December can still bring some of the coldest days of the winter. A few days of Arctic cold can be followed by a sudden thaw, then another freeze. By the end of the month, those changes may barely show up in the average temperature. For Canadians, these swings can matter more than the monthly average. Rain falling on snow, followed by freezing temperatures, can turn roads and sidewalks into ice. Sudden thaws can increase the risk of local flooding, while sharp cold spells can strain heating systems, power grids and the people least able to stay warm. December 2026 could remind us that winter is not just about how cold it gets, but how quickly the weather can change. As El Niño and the polar vortex influence Canada’s weather, the question is not simply how cold December will be. It is how quickly conditions might change, and whether we’re ready when they do. articles.content: Over the past 18 months, the Canadian government has committed record levels of funding to national defence . It has advanced major military procurement projects, expanded international defence partnerships and introduced new institutions, strategies and policies. These initiatives are aimed at rebuilding the Canadian Armed Forces and strengthening Canada’s defence industrial base. Yet a critical element of this effort remains largely absent: improving public understanding of the threats facing Canada and the rationale behind these investments. Without a more defence-literate population, sustaining this historical level of spending may prove just as challenging as securing the political commitments that made them possible. What is defence literacy? Defence literacy refers to the public’s understanding of two critical dimensions of national security: The threats facing Canada, ranging from conventional military activity, such as long-range missile attacks and an increased Russian and Chinese military presence in the Arctic and North Atlantic, to unconventional or grey-zone threats that extend beyond the battlefield. The policies, institutions and actions through which the government seeks to address these threats. For decades, national defence received little attention in Canadian public debate, owing in part to a relatively stable world order and American security guarantees. This false sense of security, however, has left Canadians with a significant blind spot. According to a 2021 Department of National Defence survey , four in 10 Canadians could not identify a specific threat to Canada’s security or sovereignty. Similarly, a 2026 survey commissioned by the Canadian Security Intelligence Service found that 35 per cent of Canadians could not name an agency responsible for investigating national security threats. Why it matters This deficit in defence literacy is more than just a knowledge gap. It reflects a longstanding failure to take national security seriously or fully understand its implications. Addressing this shortcoming, then, is important for at least four reasons: 1. Failing to do so undermines democratic accountability. Defence literacy should not be confused with defence advocacy: its purpose is not to persuade Canadians to support specific policies or military expenditures. Rather, it equips them with the knowledge necessary to understand, scrutinize and critically evaluate the decisions being made on defence, and hold their elected officials to account for those decisions—including at the ballot box. 2. Greater defence literacy strengthens national resilience. Grey-zone activities including foreign interference, cyberattacks and disinformation target individuals, communities and institutions beyond the traditional military sphere. The public is the target , and often the first line of defence. Canada’s ability to counter these threats depends heavily on whether Canadians can recognize, respond to, and mitigate their impact. A public that understands the threats facing the country is far better equipped to do so. 3. An informed public anchors defence investment beyond episodic responses to emerging crises. Improving Canada’s military capabilities requires sustained political commitment over decades, which is far more durable if rooted in public understanding. Crisis-driven support fades once the threat passes, whereas understanding the rationale behind defence priorities outlasts changes in government. 4. Canada’s expanding defence ambitions require thousands of new soldiers, educators, researchers, entrepreneurs and public servants, all of whom have important roles to play in strengthening national security. Introducing the broader Canadian public to these opportunities is essential to cultivating the next generation of leaders and professionals. Building a more defence-literate future Strengthening defence literacy cannot fall to government alone. It requires a whole-of-society approach bringing together academia, civil society and industry, all of which are instrumental in fostering a more informed and engaged population. Government must first communicate more openly with Canadians about the threats facing the country and the measures being taken to address them. Canada’s new National Security Strategy is a start in recognizing this need, but more must be done. Canada should learn from its Nordic allies, who treat public awareness and preparedness as central to national security. Sweden, for example, has distributed guidance to households explaining how to prepare for crises and war, while Finland has adopted a comprehensive security model emphasizing co-operation between government, businesses, civil society and citizens. Think tanks, universities and civil society organizations are also integral also in making defence and security issues accessible to the public. Through research, public conferences, media, educational initiatives and opportunities for dialogue, these institutions translate complex policy issues into informed public debate. In my work at the CDA Institute , a Canadian defence and security think tank, I see the value of these efforts firsthand, and of a further one: investing in young Canadians. Through student conferences, mentorship programmes, internships and student-led initiatives, we help cultivate the next generation of defence and security leaders. Read more: How the Canadian Armed Forces could help solve the youth employment crisis Industry, too, has a role in helping Canadians understand how investments in national defence are inextricably tied to more job creation, technological innovation and economic prosperity. As Canada undertakes its biggest increase in defence spending since the Second World War , it cannot afford to neglect the importance of an informed public. These investments only stand a chance of being sustained over time if accompanied by an equally strong commitment to helping Canadians understand why they are so important. Canada’s long-term security depends on both. Kevin Budning is the Director of Scientific Research at the CDA Institute.

articles.content: Indigenous notions of relationality and reciprocity offer a way of understanding knowledge that goes beyond what technology can produce. (Wikimedia Commons/Thomas Melad) , CC BY-NC-ND Universities, long entrusted with teaching, research and knowledge production, are confronting one of their most significant challenges: The rising use of artificial intelligence . As AI technologies advance, they can perform tasks once considered the exclusive domain of humans. The implications extend beyond concerns about plagiarism and academic misconduct. As UNESCO has acknowledged , generative AI raises questions about the importance of human participation in knowledge production. For universities, these developments invite an uncomfortable question : If AI can produce knowledge more efficiently, what makes human contributions to knowledge production valuable? The changing nature of knowledge production Recent developments in mathematics demonstrate how consequential this question might be. In September 2026, OpenAI announced that an AI system had produced a proposed solution to one aspect of the Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness problem, one of mathematics’ celebrated Millennium Prize problems . The Navier-Stokes problem concerns the mathematical description of fluid motion and whether certain equations can produce solutions that become unbounded. Although formal recognition of the proposed solution is pending, the announcement represents a development in AI’s capacity to contribute to mathematical discovery. Read more: AI has solved a host of big maths problems – here’s why this threatens the whole field of mathematics Achievements like this may challenge assumptions about how knowledge is produced. AI can now produce mathematical proofs and generate original research across disciplines. Universities may therefore need to reconsider what distinguishes human intellectual contributions from those of AI. These concerns are not confined to mathematics. Research demonstrates that AI may complicate conventional approaches to academic assessment, authorship and integrity. However, responding to these developments primarily through regulation and restrictions risks overlooking a more important opportunity. Fundamentally, universities should reconsider the value they assign to human lived experience as a source of knowledge. Understanding lived experience Lived experience refers to the knowledge and understanding people develop through their encounters with the world. It encompasses more than simply having experiences. It involves interpreting those experiences, assigning meaning to them and drawing upon them to understand ourselves and others . Patrick O'Leary and Ming-sum Tsui , social work researchers from Australia and Hong Kong, emphasize the importance of recognizing lived experience as a source of expertise. They argue that lived experience contributes to meaningful relationships and professional practice. Their discussion offers an important insight for universities: Knowledge is not necessarily confined to information that can be collected, analyzed and reproduced . It can also emerge from the meanings people develop through participation in the world. This distinction is especially important when considering Onkwehón:we (Indigenous) understandings of knowledge. What universities can learn from Onkwehón:we For Onkwehón:we, (a Kanien’kehá term meaning “Original Peoples”), lived experience has long been central to understanding ourselves, our world and our responsibilities. Although Onkwehón:we knowledge traditions are diverse, many emphasize that knowledge emerges through relationships among people, communities and the natural world. Onkwehón:we scholarship on relationality demonstrates how knowledge and relationships are inseparable from the people and communities in which they are developed. From this perspective, lived experience is not exclusively individual in nature. It is also collective and intergenerational. It is shaped by language, ancestral knowledge and responsibilities to others. For Onkwehón:we, knowledge may be understood through participation in relationships that extend across generations. Learning from Elders and fulfilling responsibilities within communities are not merely opportunities to acquire information. They are experiences through which knowledge becomes meaningful. Research involving Indigenous communities in Canada illustrates how relationships with the land are informed by values of respect, responsibility and reciprocity. Reciprocity is the traditional value of balanced, respectful relations with each other and with the land. These understandings challenge the assumption that knowledge can be adequately evaluated outside of the relational and experiential contexts through which it is developed. Reaffirming the purpose of universities What can universities learn from Onkwehón:we perspectives as AI becomes increasingly potent? One possibility is to place greater emphasis on lived experience within teaching, learning and research. Read more: It’s taken thousands of years, but Western science is finally catching up to Traditional Knowledge Rather than evaluating learning primarily through written work, universities could place greater emphasis upon experiential learning and community engagement. These approaches can show how knowledge shapes relationships and responsibilities. Some faculties of education, such as at Wilfrid Laurier University , already use them in parts of their programming. This would not require abandoning AI. Nor would it suggest that Indigenous knowledge traditions exist simply to resolve problems facing universities. Rather, universities can recognize that human knowledge cannot be fully understood through technology alone. Onkwehón:we scholarship already challenges universities to reconsider how their disciplinary traditions privilege certain forms of knowledge while marginalizing relational and experiential ways of knowing. Artificial intelligence makes this reconsideration increasingly urgent. An example of how scientific orientations may be reconsidered is found in the study of time. A recent study on Onkwehón:we perspectives on time explores how scientific understandings of time may be enriched by Onkwehón:we lived experiences, including seasonal cycles and relationships with the Land. Such perspectives can broaden how universities approach scientific knowledge by connecting abstract concepts with human experience. The more consequential question concerns what universities believe knowledge is for and what responsibilities accompany its creation. Onkwehón:we understandings of lived experience offer a valuable starting point. They remind us that knowledge is not simply something we produce or possess. It is also something we live, share and carry through our relationships with others . As AI begins to transform how knowledge is produced, universities have an opportunity to reaffirm the importance of human experience. Rather than an alternative to intellectual achievement, it’s an essential part of what makes knowledge meaningful. Frank Deer receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.

articles.content: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide . The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution . Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights. Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions . Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya. The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya. Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government . Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament . This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility. The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army. The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region , where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state. The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided. But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism ; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law. Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it. The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs . How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs. Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) . Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance. Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps. More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026 . Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees , it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed. It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community. Not ‘illegal immigrants’ Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine. The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice. San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine. The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice. San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
articles.title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar

articles.content: An increasing share of Canadians are reporting financial difficulties. According to Statistics Canada , 39 per cent said it was difficult or very difficult for their household to meet its financial needs in spring 2025. Younger adults were particularly likely to experience financial difficulties. These struggles were linked to deteriorating life satisfaction and declining hope for the future. Incomes remain stagnant for many Canadians while costs climb , employment uncertainties continue and social safety net programs struggle to fill the gap. These situations show how rising economic insecurity is affecting people’s lives. Economic insecurity — sometimes described as precarity, vulnerability or financial risk — refers to how individuals balance resources and costs. To better understand how economic insecurity affects Canadians across social classes, we surveyed more than 8,000 Canadians and interviewed 127 about their experiences with economic insecurity as part of the Great Canadian Class Study . By talking to people in in-depth interviews, we learned more about the factors that lead to insecurity and how participants understood these situations. The conversations also highlighted the growing divides between younger and older adults in Canada. Economic security cuts across class We began this project to investigate whether, and how, social class shapes people’s lives in Canada. We found that social class matters in myriad ways, but not always in the ways we might expect. Growing economic insecurity helps explain why. Our recently published research in the British Journal of Sociology highlights why people’s experiences and perceptions of economic insecurity must be considered when examining social class. Our survey found that younger people, unemployed people, members of lower-income households, renters and people carrying stressful levels of credit card debt were more likely to experience insecurity. They were less able to meet their monthly expenses and did not have enough savings to cover an emergency expense. Our interviews revealed that economic insecurity was not only reflected in people’s income or assets. Some homeowners, for example, described feeling financially insecure despite owning property. The rising cost of living still left them with little money to set aside for savings or emergencies. Economic security cannot always be understood through income or wealth alone. People’s ability to manage unexpected expenses and their perceptions of their financial circumstances also matter. The growing generational divide Younger Canadians experienced the most severe effects of insecurity. Despite doing “everything right” to set themselves up for stability, many expressed resignation that they would never achieve the signifiers of middle-class status that past generations had, or the security that once came with it. Education, which has historically been seen as a route to job stability and higher incomes, instead contributed to feelings of insecurity in participants. Student debt felt insurmountable and shaped participants’ decisions about whether to pursue further schooling when rising tuition costs might not be offset by higher future earnings. Home ownership, once a traditional marker of middle-class success , was also not possible for most younger participants. Rising housing costs due to the treatment of housing as an investment opportunity , the dominance of private equity and real estate investment firms and mounting debt have made home ownership increasingly difficult to attain. For those shut out of home ownership, renting brought its own uncertainties, including rent increases, evictions and frustration at not being able to build wealth. This contrasted with the experiences of some older participants, who built their lives during a time of more opportunity and lower income inequality. Decades of good-paying jobs, a stronger social assistance system and a favourable housing market provided a stronger foundation for lifelong economic security. Homes, investments, pensions and personal savings were all sources of security that could be used to mitigate unforeseen emergencies. Addressing economic insecurity Despite its pervasiveness, there are many steps governments can take to alleviate the increasing insecurity Canadians are feeling across generations. Reinvesting in the social infrastructure that provided previous generations with a strong footing would be a good place to start. This includes expanding funding for post-secondary education to address the steady declines in government grants, strengthening rent control , building more non-market housing and instituting broader tax reforms to address growing income and wealth inequality . Our study reflects a changing Canada in which even people who grew up believing that education and hard work would lead to middle-class stability are experiencing economic insecurity. The traditional promise of meritocracy rests on the idea that people who work hard, pursue education and make responsible financial decisions can improve their circumstances. However, when those efforts no longer reliably lead to financial security, that promise becomes harder to sustain. The growing disconnect between Canadians’ expectations and their lived realities suggests that the traditional path to middle-class security is becoming increasingly difficult to follow. Michelle Maroto receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC). Andrea DeKeseredy receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC).

articles.content: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families. “I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025 . “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change. For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom. For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages , including Nepali and English. Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue . A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world , though the state has not always acknowledged it . The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues . Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages . Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population . I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity . The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities. In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language , a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali. For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue . Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011 . Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk. Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues. In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown , policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support. In a 2026 study from Tanahun , one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.” Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID) , CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams. Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English , according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale. In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.” Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents , points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.” Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained. Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget , well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education . Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them. From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.” Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities. Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues . Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they. Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

articles.content: On Nov. 22, the day after COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya , Turkey, the global average temperature at noon UTC was estimated to be a record-setting 2.36 C above the pre-industrial average . Climate change is driving up global temperatures. Yet governments could not even agree to name the fossil fuels driving it. I have been a climate scientist since the late 1980s and have followed every UN climate summit since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. I cannot recall a more embarrassing failure than COP31. The first draft proposed at least US$120 billion by 2035 to help countries adapt to climate change. By Nov. 19, the figure was gone. Three years ago in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. The Nov. 16 Antalya draft said so plainly. Yet, the final proposal at COP31 still omitted any mention of fossil fuels. The European Union and small island states were right to reject it. Given the recent failure, is it time for scientists and activists to boycott COP? From early success to utter failure While COP31 collapsed without an agreement, previous UN climate talks have had successes. In the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, industrialized countries agreed to reduce their collective emissions, averaged over 2008–12, to 5.2 per cent below 1990 levels. Emissions over the 2008-12 reporting period came in 9.9 per cent below 1990 levels . In Paris in 2015 , governments agreed to hold warming “well below 2 C above pre-industrial levels” while “pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels.” Yet, in June 2026, a UN report found that the world is set to exceed the 1.5 C global warming target outlined in Paris. In 2015, governments invited the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to report back in 2018 on the impacts of 1.5 C of warming and the emissions pathways that could get us there. In future emissions pathways leading to little or no overshoot of the 1.5 C target, global net carbon dioxide emissions were required to fall roughly 45 per cent from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050. Those pathways also required removing 100 to 1,000 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere over the century (so-called negative emissions) using technology that had yet to be developed. The authors spelled out the difficulties. The key government takeaway was that meeting the 1.5 C target could still be achieved. What struck me was how little those models resembled the world in which people make decisions. You can write carbon removal into a model. Somebody still has to find the land, build the equipment and pay to operate it. You don’t build a coal plant today to tear it down tomorrow. The utility has debt to repay and communities need power. What if we stayed home? Andrew Weaver on BBC News discussing COP31. Scientists, environmentalists and youth groups should boycott the next COP. I further think scientists should also consider walking away from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessments. I was a lead author on four of them . I know what that invitation means to a young scientist, yet at some point, the scientific community needs to speak out as a collective. And those of us who have already had the privilege of working on IPCC assessments ought to speak first — and loudest. The Paris Agreement showed how readily governments can use our willingness to buy time. Ministers agreed on a temperature, asked us what it would mean if the world exceeded it, then continued exploiting fossil fuels regardless. Climate change has become a global tragedy of the commons. Fossil-fuel producers earn money selling their products while sharing the climatic cost with everyone else. Countries and tech companies are incentivized to race ahead with artificial intelligence, regardless of the environmental risks the rest of us inherit . And in our politics, climate change has become subsumed into a culture war where politics rail against green policies regardless of the facts. While Canada’s delegates were in Antalya, Ottawa committed $200 million to expand planned production at Woodfibre LNG, a liquefied natural gas export terminal in British Columbia. With decisions like that, the world is on course to even exceed 2 C of global warming. So, let governments go to the next COP and explain the empty seats. Save the airfare, the emissions and two weeks of time better spent elsewhere. Instead, use a fraction of that time to ask your representatives about the tangible action they are taking to tackle climate change. Andrew Weaver receives funding from NSERC and NRCan. He has previously served as an MLA and leader of the BC Green Party.
