articles.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy

articles.content: Canada’s National Food Security Strategy aims to improve food security, affordability and to support locally grown and produced food. This 10-year, $3.2 billion strategy includes historic investments in domestic food production, processing and distribution. The strategy also recognizes that rural, remote and northern communities face distinct challenges that require targeted policy responses. But whether the strategy achieves its goals depends on how it’s implemented. As part of this strategy, the $1 billion federal Food-Link Fund was launched in October 2026. It consists of two programs: The Food Terminal Fund that supports large-scale wholesale food terminals, which are typically located in major urban centres and serve broad regional markets. The Food Hub Program , which aims to build storage, processing, aggregation and distribution infrastructure closer to producers that are typically located in smaller communities and rural regions. Rural considerations The two funding streams recognize that rural communities often face different transportation, distribution and infrastructure challenges and therefore require different supports. Evidence from other policy areas, like public transit and housing, shows that programs designed specifically for rural communities can be more effective. Read more: Is Canada finally investing in its rural communities? What funding for rural transit reveals The Common Ground Network released a research brief recommending ways to better understand the full range of services that Food Hubs provide to better position them for success within the National Food Security Strategy. Applying these recommendations to the Food-Link Fund can also help strengthen its impact in rural communities. The recommendations also reveal several potential challenges that policymakers should address. What does the Food-Link Fund get right? A “food hub” is a broad term that covers many community-based food activities . Past programs supporting food hubs often used narrow definitions of what counted as a food hub . In contrast, the Food-Link Fund focuses on desired outcomes. As described by the program guide : “Activities must be related to expanding and modernizing the existing network of food hubs and distribution systems to improve aggregation, processing, storage, and distribution options.” This flexibility allows communities to design projects that meet local needs. There are many local food security initiatives that already do these kinds of activities, even if they don’t call themselves food hubs. These include food co-operatives, solidarity supermarkets, independent grocers, farmers’ markets, food banks and other non-profit food distribution centres. The Food-Link Fund can support both new and existing initiatives, and allows applicants to build on what already exists. For-profits, non-profits and Indigenous organizations are all eligible to apply. Including non-profits is particularly important because many already play a key role in food distribution. The two-step application process may make it easier for organizations with less capacity to apply. If an expression of interest is approved, applicants have up to one year to prepare a full proposal. The fund also gives projects time to become stable and grow, offering up to $25 million per project over 10 years. This differs from many past programs that offered one-time funding and short timelines that have produced precarious conditions , making it harder for food hubs to maintain themselves and grow. What does the Food-Link Fund miss? Rural, remote and northern communities differ in terms of their size, accessibility and other place-specific traits. Needs and capacity can differ significantly. Unfortunately, some aspects of the Food-Link Fund are problematic for some rural places. The program’s desired outcomes include increased food distribution infrastructure, increased use of hubs by small and medium-sized businesses and stronger supply chains. But it pays less attention to social impacts and measures of success . For example, does food become more affordable or accessible? Are more people connected to health and social services? Do staff and volunteers gain valuable training and work experience? Is culturally appropriate food easier to access? Are local food systems better able to respond to disruptions? Read more: Canada’s new strategy won’t solve food insecurity or the health issues it creates Under the current program criteria, improvements in these areas don’t seem to count heavily in funding decisions. Yet food hubs are not simply places that move and store food. They also build relationships, trust and local capacity that help communities prevent and respond to crises. Financial sustainability is another key assessment criterion. Applicants must demonstrate that projects can continue operating without ongoing government support. While this may seem reasonable, it can disadvantage smaller and more remote communities where issues of accessibility and economies of scale mean the market economy is the least functional. Market failure can also be caused or made worse by poverty — impacting both rural and urban communities. Ironically, the communities facing market failures are often the same communities facing the greatest barriers to food access and distribution. These challenges are made worse by cost-sharing requirements. Applicants must secure 50 per cent of project costs, or 40 per cent for projects led by Indigenous or equity-deserving groups. Communities with the greatest financial needs are often the least able to provide matching funds. Securing matching funds The National Food Security Strategy recognizes that rural, remote and northern communities face unique food access challenges. Yet the Food-Link Fund’s emphasis on economic performance may create barriers precisely where needs are greatest. Some worthwhile projects may never reach the application stage because their goals are primarily social or because they cannot secure matching funds. As a result, the program may favour applicants or communities that are already well positioned to succeed rather than those facing the greatest food security challenges. Sarah-Patricia Breen receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, the Province of British Columbia, ETSI-BC, and Mitacs. She is the past president of the Canadian Rural Revitalization Foundation. In her research she works closely with local partners, including the Kootenay Food Council. Jacob Kearey-Moreland is a researcher with the Common Ground Network, a project funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC), in partnership with Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada (AAFC). He also serves as a volunteer board member with The Sharing Place Food Centre in Orillia, Ontario, Canada. Sara Edge is the Arrell Chair in Food, Policy & Society and receives funding from the Arrell Food Institute at the University of Guelph. She works with community partners that provide various food programs often through hub-based infrastructure.

articles.content: The latest episode of Saturday Night Live (SNL) featured a viral comedy sketch in which a series of men confidently explain that their sisters will shoulder the burden of caring for their aging parents. The sketch is funny because it’s so familiar. In just three minutes of satire, it captures a reality many women know all too well: when parents need care, daughters are often expected to step in while sons step aside. Social media reactions were swift. Responses ranged from “I am sister” to comments on social media calling on men to start doing their fair share. Beneath the humour lies an uncomfortable truth about who provides care and the growing pressures facing families as the population ages. The SNL sketch resonates because it reflects a private family reality that has become a public policy issue. The burden on women Globally, the International Labour Organization estimates 708 million women are unable to join the labour force because of unpaid care responsibilities . According to the United Nations, women around the world do 16 billion hours of unpaid care work every day. Cleaning, cooking and looking after the elderly are among the essential daily tasks predominantly performed by women and girls. In Canada, data show that women continue to shoulder most unpaid caregiving responsibilities . Men accounted for only 20 per cent of caregiving in the early 2000s, rising to 42 per cent by 2018. This progress is worth celebrating. As is the case globally, the Statistics Canada report also showed the intensity and type of the unpaid care remains highly gendered. Women are more likely to provide personal care, including bathing, dressing, feeding and toileting, while men are more likely to undertake home maintenance and outdoor work. Women also spend more time caregiving, averaging 10 hours a week compared with six hours for men. And this is happening at a time when several demographic forces are coming to a head. Globally, fertility rates are falling . More women are participating in the labour force around the world than ever before . Canada, for example, is experiencing its highest-ever rate of women aged 25-54 in the workforce, at 85 per cent . Taken together, these trends mean families are getting smaller and women are less available to serve as unpaid caregivers. Families therefore need to work together to make the division of labour between members more equitable. Women carers need to ask for the supports they need, and men need to step up, recognizing that care tasks, like cooking and medical management, are learned and can be taught. The role of the workplace But one of the most important places left to make the changes needed is the workplace. My research advocates for more carer-inclusive workplaces and caregiver-friendly employers. In Canada in 2018, one in 20 employees who were working full-time while also providing unpaid care to an adult left or intended to leave paid employment. Another one in seven worked fewer hours for pay. The consequences can be significant, particularly for women. Leaving a job or moving from full-time to part-time work can negatively affect health, income, pension, benefits, career progression, social networks and quality of life. Carer-friendly workplaces recognize that many of their employees are also managing unpaid care to an adult . These employers have policies and practices in place to support and accommodate employee-caregivers. These include flex time, telework, job sharing, paid or unpaid leave, government supports, benefits and caregiver support groups. Research shows there is a strong business case for these kinds of care-inclusive practices. A report from the American Association of Retired People found that for every dollar invested, employers can expect an average return of between two and four dollars. There are also increases in productivity, reduced absenteeism, lower presenteeism — when people are showing up to work but not really engaged — as well as improved employee retention and reduced recruitment costs. Supporting caregivers In Canada, provincial and jurisdictional supports are more readily available now than ever before, including those from the Ontario Caregivers Organization or the Family Caregivers of British Columbia . McMaster University in Hamilton, Ont., has partnered with the Canadian Standards Association to build a voluntary Carer-Inclusive and Accommodating Organizations Standard and handbook, “Helping worker-carers in your organization .” These tools will hopefully encourage workplaces across the country to better support employee-caregivers. Read more: Women caregivers need more support to manage their responsibilities and well-being The SNL sketch resonated because it transformed a familiar family tension into comedy. But for millions of women who are juggling both employment and an increasing unpaid care load, the issue is no laughing matter. Employers must recognize the ethical imperative and the business case for carer-inclusive workplace policies. This is critical as public health-care systems face increasing pressure, work lives grow busier and the population continues to age. Otherwise, we risk seeing more women burn out or leave the workforce altogether, undermining progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal of achieving gender equality . Allison Williams is a Tier 1 Canadian Research Chair in the Care Economy, Aging & Policy, funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research. The Partnership Research Program she leads is funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) and is entitled “The Care Economy, Aging and Policy: A Partnership Approach” (File Number: 895-2026-1023).

articles.content: A warning sign at Bartlett's Point Park in Corner Brook, NL. (Josie Wittmer) , CC BY The popular new Netflix thriller series Below portrays life in coastal Newfoundland and a frightening presence in the water that turns out to be a giant squid. However, the show’s tagline, “something’s in the water,” also speaks to another alarming reality in the water for many Newfoundland communities: sewage. Municipalities across the island of Newfoundland struggle to manage and dispose of raw sewage. The persistence of sewage effluent in local waters is experienced as a localized environmental threat, an infrastructural inequality, a burden on local finances and labour and a source of embarrassment in Newfoundland’s cities and towns that do not have the infrastructures to comply with federal wastewater management regulations. In a new SSHRC-funded project , I am exploring the mismatches between wastewater policies and local experiences of sewage infrastructure challenges in Newfoundland. Policy-infrastructure mismatches In Canada, wastewater is regulated at the federal level under the Fisheries Act by the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations (WSER) . The regulations came into effect in 2015 and require secondary-level wastewater treatment (for example, facilities using biological processes to remove organic matter and suspended solids) to meet national quality standards and reduce threats to fish and human health. Yet, in Newfoundland and Labrador, 186 of 212 wastewater discharge points regulated by the WSER have no treatment at all . In 2021, only three per cent of Newfoundland and Labrador wastewater systems complied with the WSER . Map of Canada’s Effluent Quality results under the WSER (2021 results): Systems meeting WSER requirements at least 75 per cent of the time. (Generated by the author, November 2026) Under the WSER, non-compliant municipalities must apply for “transitional authorizations (TAs),” or permissions to continue polluting. TAs require regular sampling, analyses in authorized labs, acute-lethality (fish kill) tests and the submission of this data to a federal portal. However, many smaller communities with few municipal staff and small budgets struggle to finance, administer and monitor their water to meet these reporting requirements and continue polluting with permission. Infrastructural inequities Newfoundland communities of various sizes struggle to bridge the gap between the enforcement of federal environmental policies and their sewage management realities on the ground. For example, the City of Corner Brook releases over 20,000 square metres (approximately eight Olympic-sized swimming pools) of raw, untreated sewage effluent into the ocean every day. The city has struggled for more than a decade to obtain provincial and federal funds to build a secondary treatment facility. The estimated cost of the facility required in Corner Brook is $120-130 million . In early 2026, the city was served with an environmental directive by armed Department of Fisheries and Oceans officers who levied fines and threatened criminal charges because of the volume of effluent the city is releasing into the Bay of Islands. In the meantime, Corner Brook pays $60,000 a year to an authorized private lab to analyze their polluted water samples in order to provide the required data to the federal government’s portal. Small communities across the island are also dealing with big sewage issues. In addition to lacking wastewater treatment facilities, many municipalities have aging sewage infrastructure and experience frequent sewage blockages, line breaks and overflow. For small towns with an increased population during warmer months due to seasonal residents, workers and tourists, these challenges compound as the sewage increases. The town clerk of a community with around 1,000 residents recently estimated that 30 per cent of the town’s budget could be spent elsewhere if not for the costs of water and sewage infrastructure repairs and wastewater monitoring . Contracting out wastewater sampling For many small municipalities, producing data to keep a transitional authorization can be a labour burden, logistically challenging and expensive. Third-party companies are stepping in to fill the gap between regulations and municipal realities by selling wastewater sampling, lab and consulting services for a fee. In a recent interview, an elected official in a small western Newfoundland town with a population of less than 500 residents told me: “When you see the (company) van drive through town, you know there’s also an $8,000 invoice coming.” A 2019 report in The Telegram estimated that 80 per cent of Newfoundland municipalities contract out their wastewater sampling and analysis to one firm , Biomaxx Environmental. Following global trends in wastewater monitoring and the growing presence of private sector solutions for municipal wastewater challenges , I suggest the current enforcement of WSER is creating the conditions for community wastewater challenges to become a source of profit. In other words, wastewater is emerging as a place where private companies are creating a market for themselves in municipalities struggling to comply with regulations that were not made with their infrastructure realities in mind. ‘Get back from the water’ In Below , Josh Hartnett’s Calvin Penney runs through a community event shouting for everyone to “get back from the water!” When watching the scene, I was reminded of stories I’ve heard from municipal staff and residents of Newfoundland communities running up to tourists to tell them to stay out of the waters near outfalls, where pipes, drains or sewers discharge wastewater into bodies of water. One such incident included a cruise ship passenger clad in snorkel equipment, wading into the waters from the beach directly in front of Corner Brook’s largest sewage outfall. Untreated sewage — along with the disconnect between federal regulations and local infrastructure — is a major obstacle in communities that still lack wastewater treatment. Local sewage challenges also reach far beyond environmental pollution and municipal budgets, affecting community planning, tourism, public health, recreation, local food sovereignty and access to shoreline food sources. Josie Wittmer receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC). This research is funded by a SSHRC Insight Development Grant (2026-2028).

The persistence of sewage effluent in local waters is experienced as a localized environmental threat, an infrastructural inequality, a burden on local finances and labour and a source of embarrassment in Newfoundland’s cities and towns that do not have the infrastructures to comply with federal wastewater management regulations. In a new SSHRC-funded project , I am exploring the mismatches between wastewater policies and local experiences of sewage infrastructure challenges in Newfoundland. Policy-infrastructure mismatches In Canada, wastewater is regulated at the federal level under the Fisheries Act by the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations (WSER) . The regulations came into effect in 2015 and require secondary-level wastewater treatment (for example, facilities using biological processes to remove organic matter and suspended solids) to meet national quality standards and reduce threats to fish and human health. Yet, in Newfoundland and Labrador, 186 of 212 wastewater discharge points regulated by the WSER have no treatment at all . In 2021, only three per cent of Newfoundland and Labrador wastewater systems complied with the WSER . Map of Canada’s Effluent Quality results under the WSER (2021 results): Systems meeting WSER requirements at least 75 per cent of the time. (Generated by the author, November 2026) Under the WSER, non-compliant municipalities must apply for “transitional authorizations (TAs),” or permissions to continue polluting. TAs require regular sampling, analyses in authorized labs, acute-lethality (fish kill) tests and the submission of this data to a federal portal. However, many smaller communities with few municipal staff and small budgets struggle to finance, administer and monitor their water to meet these reporting requirements and continue polluting with permission. Infrastructural inequities Newfoundland communities of various sizes struggle to bridge the gap between the enforcement of federal environmental policies and their sewage management realities on the ground. For example, the City of Corner Brook releases over 20,000 square metres (approximately eight Olympic-sized swimming pools) of raw, untreated sewage effluent into the ocean every day. The city has struggled for more than a decade to obtain provincial and federal funds to build a secondary treatment facility. The estimated cost of the facility required in Corner Brook is $120-130 million . In early 2026, the city was served with an environmental directive by armed Department of Fisheries and Oceans officers who levied fines and threatened criminal charges because of the volume of effluent the city is releasing into the Bay of Islands. In the meantime, Corner Brook pays $60,000 a year to an authorized private lab to analyze their polluted water samples in order to provide the required data to the federal government’s portal. Small communities across the island are also dealing with big sewage issues. In addition to lacking wastewater treatment facilities, many municipalities have aging sewage infrastructure and experience frequent sewage blockages, line breaks and overflow. For small towns with an increased population during warmer months due to seasonal residents, workers and tourists, these challenges compound as the sewage increases. The town clerk of a community with around 1,000 residents recently estimated that 30 per cent of the town’s budget could be spent elsewhere if not for the costs of water and sewage infrastructure repairs and wastewater monitoring . Contracting out wastewater sampling For many small municipalities, producing data to keep a transitional authorization can be a labour burden, logistically challenging and expensive. Third-party companies are stepping in to fill the gap between regulations and municipal realities by selling wastewater sampling, lab and consulting services for a fee. In a recent interview, an elected official in a small western Newfoundland town with a population of less than 500 residents told me: “When you see the (company) van drive through town, you know there’s also an $8,000 invoice coming.” A 2019 report in The Telegram estimated that 80 per cent of Newfoundland municipalities contract out their wastewater sampling and analysis to one firm , Biomaxx Environmental. Following global trends in wastewater monitoring and the growing presence of private sector solutions for municipal wastewater challenges , I suggest the current enforcement of WSER is creating the conditions for community wastewater challenges to become a source of profit. In other words, wastewater is emerging as a place where private companies are creating a market for themselves in municipalities struggling to comply with regulations that were not made with their infrastructure realities in mind. ‘Get back from the water’ In Below , Josh Hartnett’s Calvin Penney runs through a community event shouting for everyone to “get back from the water!” When watching the scene, I was reminded of stories I’ve heard from municipal staff and residents of Newfoundland communities running up to tourists to tell them to stay out of the waters near outfalls, where pipes, drains or sewers discharge wastewater into bodies of water. One such incident included a cruise ship passenger clad in snorkel equipment, wading into the waters from the beach directly in front of Corner Brook’s largest sewage outfall. Untreated sewage — along with the disconnect between federal regulations and local infrastructure — is a major obstacle in communities that still lack wastewater treatment. Local sewage challenges also reach far beyond environmental pollution and municipal budgets, affecting community planning, tourism, public health, recreation, local food sovereignty and access to shoreline food sources. articles.content: Liberal members of Parliament in Canada recently agreed to amend the controversial proposed legislation, Bill C-39 , that critics say would undermine environmental protections and Indigenous and labour rights if passed into law. The amendments come days after protests against the bill took place in cities across Canada. The proposed legislation, called the Building Canada Strong Act, aims to fast-track development projects such as pipelines and mines. In line with that push, the Canadian government recently turned its attention to reviving interest in Arctic offshore oil and gas. The fall 2026 budget earmarked millions of dollars for northern oil and gas governance . Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced plans for consultations and capacity-building in the western Arctic, with an eye toward lifting a federal moratorium on offshore oil and gas extraction in the Canadian Arctic . But will this surge of political support lead to hydrocarbon production in the region? Arctic oil and gas moratorium In 2016, the Canadian and American governments implemented a moratorium on Arctic drilling . The ban was meant to support climate commitments, study the environmental risks and develop parks and protected areas in line with international commitments to preserve lands and waters . The ban’s ultimate promise was to build a sustainable Arctic economy , in partnership with other Arctic nations. But its reception in the North was mixed. Concern about missed potential economic opportunities came with concern from others that the ban didn’t go far enough . A CBC News report on the Canadian government reviewing the Arctic oil and gas drilling ban. Bill C-39 has been criticized for the potential limits it would place on environmental protections, Indigenous and labour rights in the name of “ building Canada strong .” Arctic oil and gas opportunities appear to be one of the target resources of this policy. The history of Arctic offshore oil and gas extraction in Canada can tell us a lot about how these proposals might take shape in the present and future. The history of Canada’s attempt to build an oil and gas economy in Arctic waters is, for the most part, a history of failed projects. Expensive, complex and risky Why did Arctic oil and gas projects fail? The most obvious answer is a combination of climate, geography and the risks these projects produce. In short, it is hugely expensive, technically complex and ecologically risky to move oil and gas from Arctic waters to southern refineries and markets. Uncertainty around jurisdiction and local community benefits further complicates the question of Arctic oil and gas . On a broader scale, interest in offshore hydrocarbon resources in Arctic Canada tends to wax and wane alongside shifting geopolitical tensions and instabilities in oil-producing regions globally. The Berger Inquiry into the Mackenzie Valley pipeline unfolded in the shadow of the 1973 oil embargo and Arab-Israeli War. The 1979 Iranian Revolution and oil shocks reinvigorated pressure for Arctic oil and gas production, with several Canadian and international energy companies submitting proposals for offshore production in the Beaufort Sea . A revived proposal for a natural gas pipeline in the Mackenzie Valley was assessed in the context of surging energy prices tied to the 2003 invasion of Iraq by the United States. In each case, global prices for oil and gas dropped before the proposed projects began, rendering production commercially unviable. Science fiction infrastructure dreams This geopolitical intrigue has made Arctic offshore oil and gas into a “stranded resource” — it’s easy to see the appeal of an untapped reserve. To solve the Arctic oil and gas riddle, engineers and oil executives have dreamed up a dizzying array of technological adaptations and infrastructures to move oil and gas to southern markets. Drill rigs on floating ice islands of sand dredged from the ocean floor. Oil tankers split in half and towed into the Beaufort Sea. A type of 12-propeller plane, nicknamed the Brute Lifter , ferrying oil to Edmonton in the fuselage. Nuclear submarines full of oil sailing under the ice. Arctic island-hopping gas pipelines . These and more science-fictional infrastructure dreams were all in the mix at one point or another. Similar ideas will have to be brought into being if the Canadian government proceeds with further exploration of Arctic oil and gas. Arctic resources as crisis response The current push has many of the hallmarks of previous attempts to drill in Arctic waters. Carney’s interest in lifting the federal moratorium on offshore oil and gas extraction similarly responds to geopolitical instability and proposes huge, “dreamy” infrastructure investment. In this case, the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran are driving Canadian politicians to once again look to Arctic hydrocarbons as a crisis response . Projects of “ national interest ” — such as an invigorated oil and gas economy in the western Arctic and Beaufort Sea or the Port of Churchill Plus in northern Manitoba — are likely to gain traction. Time, money and work will be invested into consultations and assessments, including significant resources and labour from Indigenous organizations and communities. The issue will likely once again prove divisive within and between Indigenous communities and organizations, leading to political conflict over proposed exploration and extraction activities. The end result is likely to be the same as previous attempts to extract oil and gas from Arctic waters in Canada. Projects will face the usual insurmountable economic, environmental and political barriers to development, and interest in Arctic oil and gas will once again wane. The last well drilled in the Beaufort Sea was in 2006. It remains to be seen if the Carney government can surmount the social, environmental and geopolitical barriers that led to previous failures to build an oil and gas economy in Canada’s Arctic. Jonathan Peyton receives funding from SSHRC. Warren Bernauer receives funding from the Canada Research Chair Program.

articles.content: A new day, a new cyberattack. The most recent is an attack that impacted 178 major websites, including those of the BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, Salesforce and Equifax . This follows a series of cyberattacks and disruptions over the last two months — most notably on supermarkets throughout Europe. A series of attacks in France during October raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 50 C in more than 350 supermarkets. Overnight, large amounts of food spoiled, equipment overheated and fires were reported. Affected stores had to discard food and temporarily close. Similar attacks and disruptions were then reported across several countries in November, including Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg. In all of these cases, hackers remotely reprogrammed internet-connected temperature controls. They switched evaporators to defrost mode, raising temperatures beyond safety limits. These simple changes impacted physical equipment, businesses and people. How will the next cyberattack unfold, and where? Our industrial critical infrastructure offers many targets — from blood banks to chemical manufacturing plants , nuclear reactors , aviation and other transportation systems and wastewater treatment facilities . The potential consequences are vast. Our team at the Cyber Security Evaluation and Assurance (CyberSEA) research lab at Carleton University has simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility to identify the most serious consequences. We have also mapped out seven dimensions for understanding cyberattack impacts . The vulnerability of critical infrastructure Critical infrastructure refers to 10 broad sectors including energy and utilities, water, health, transportation and food. Systems in these sectors provide essential services. Connecting the systems to the internet improves efficiency, but can also expose such services to modern cybersecurity threats. Cybersecurity analysis tends to focus on attacks and how they could have been prevented. Cyberattack impact analysis , on the other hand, looks at what happens after a system is compromised — which operations are disrupted, how the effects spread and who or what might be harmed. A supermarket is more than its refrigerator temperature controls. It’s a system involving food, equipment, employees, customers, business continuity and public confidence. Similarly, a water utility contains pumps and software but also protects a wider system of treatment processes, public health, the environment and access to safe water. Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure radiate impact through all of our lives. Learning from wastewater systems Wastewater treatment provides a good example of the far-reaching consequences of a cyberattack. When we simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility , we found this could force equipment to operate excessively or near safety limits. It could also increase chemical consumption, push the plant into costly contingency modes or interfere with chemical dosing. The most serious scenario involved discharging under-treated wastewater into the city’s river. This might seem extreme, but something similar has already happened. In 2000, a former employee attacked the Maroochy Shire wastewater system in Australia . He remotely interfered with sewage pumping stations, preventing pumps and alarms from operating properly. Over three months, millions of gallons of untreated sewage entered waterways and local parks. 7 dimensions of impact Our recent research identifies seven dimensions for understanding the consequences of cyberattacks. The supermarket attacks across Europe illustrate all seven. Operational impacts occur when a system cannot perform its intended function, while physical impacts involve changes or damage to equipment and materials. In the supermarkets, altered temperature controls disrupted food preservation, equipment overheated and food spoiled. The consequences can then spread beyond the system. Safety impacts expose people to hazards, such as fires or unsafe food. Environmental impacts harm air, water, land or ecosystems — such as discarded food creating additional waste. Economic impacts include lost products, equipment repairs, downtime and lost customers. Broader consequences may also emerge. Societal impacts disrupt communities or their access to important goods and services, such as fresh food. Reputational impacts arise when people lose confidence in an organization or service, for example, due to concerns about food safety. These dimensions are connected. One disrupted operation can produce several impacts at once, some continuing after the technical problem has been resolved. Preparing for consequences We may not know how the next cyberattack will unfold. But we can prepare for unsafe water, damaged equipment, environmental harm, interrupted services, financial losses and diminished public trust. Impact analysis helps decision-makers ask practical questions: Which consequences are unacceptable? Where are additional safeguards needed? Who must respond when safety or environmental harm occurs? Which services must be restored first? The goal is not merely to keep attackers out of computer systems. It is to keep essential services working when cyber-defences fail. articles.content: Ontario Education Minister Paul Calandra recently discussed concerns about whether Ontario’s “inclusion model” in education was working . The comments were made after a social policy committee hearing where the minister was asked about gaps in funding special education needs . Concerns about inclusion models are in the news elsewhere too. But researchers note a lack of agreement around what inclusion means and importantly , what it implies for education policy and student services . In Ontario, depending on who you ask, the discussion around an “inclusion model” and its success or failure could involve the increased reports of violence in the classroom , funds to support students with exceptionalities , class size, educator resources , student attendance or other important topics. More clarity is needed in Ontario around what we mean by models of inclusive education in terms of where, how and what students learn. Where, how, what students learn Researchers note that the essential element of a model is its usefulness for a specific purpose. For example, the map of my university helps new students find their way from one building to another, but it’s not useful for finding the coziest study spots. A map or model of inclusive education would provide clear guidelines of what this is, and what it isn’t, and what should be expected in the education of students with exceptionalities. While Ontario has standards and definitions that address specialized supports for students with exceptionalities, currently, decisions for the 360,000-plus students with special needs are made on a case-by-case basis. A clear model could mean more guidance from the province and collective agreement on expectations for educational decisions. What guides inclusive education? Inclusive Education Canada emphasizes student belonging and value with a focus on meaningful engagement of students with disabilities “alongside their peers without disabilities.” UNESCO describes a model of inclusive education that guides “equitable access to quality learning.” It envisions a focus on educator collaboration, flexible and individualized curricula and supports in unified learning environments. Federally, Canada has committed to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities . This includes a pledge to promote access to support in general education environments enabled by appropriate teacher training. In Ontario, the Education Act’s Regulation 181/98 , pertaining to “Identification and placement of exceptional pupils,” assumes children should be placed in a general education class with appropriate supports before considering specialized placement options. The provincial Ministry of Education’s Policy/Program Memorandum 119 defines inclusive education as being: “Based on the principles of acceptance and inclusion of all students. Students see themselves reflected in their curriculum, their physical surroundings and the broader environment.” Special education policy in Ontario requires boards to make note of their special education “service-delivery model” for students with exceptionalities, within their ministry-reviewed annual special education plans . However, the requirement doesn’t ask boards how services for students relate to fostering inclusion. Inclusion models have evolved Over time, inclusion models in general have evolved . The focus shifted from where students learn (from special education to general education classrooms) to where and how students learn. This change has involved adding specialized and inclusive teaching strategies in general classroom settings. Current models combine a focus on where, how and what students learn. “What” implies robust academic expectations and sufficient support for academic achievement. Ontario decisions about where students learn — termed “educational placement decisions” — are made by the Identification, Placement, and Review Committees . These include at least three members (for example: a school principal, students 16 years or older, a student’s parents and other relevant school staff). Research from my colleagues and me shows that educational placement in general settings has increased over time, but not for all students. Students with behavioural exceptionalities did not see increased placements in inclusive settings. Students identified with developmental disabilities or who are deaf or hard of hearing had some increased placements in general classrooms, but still had the lowest placements there. Researchers have documented the subjective and contextual nature of such decisions. Like other researchers , we also found that external factors , including school board and student age, were significant predictors of educational placement decisions. Read more: Navigating special education labels is complex, and it matters for education equity How students learn: support decisions Ontario’s Learning for All policy promoted general inclusive strategies such as Universal Design for Learning and Differentiated Instruction. But support decisions are made by a student’s educators and recorded and tracked in the student’s Individual Education Plan (IEP). Ontario’s latest audit report and research on teacher training in the province point to problems in teacher education, as well as resources and practices that can negatively influence developing IEPs and ultimately student learning supports. Read more: Children on individual education plans: What parents need to know, and 4 questions they should ask What students learn The Ontario curriculum is designed to describe essential learning expectations for knowledge and skills for all students across the province. Students with special education needs may receive supports accessing the curriculum through educational accommodations. These increase support but don’t change the learning expectation. However, some students with disabilities access the curriculum in a modified format: learning expectations are simplified. Modifications can be helpful to identify learning gaps and provide high-intensity supports. However, there are concerns that this approach is overused, as noted in the Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read inquiry report . Beyond curricular modification, students with exceptionalities may also participate in alternate programs, addressing, for example, life skills. Similar to placement and supports, educational content access is determined on a case-by-case basis for students with special education. For some students, like those with a learning disability, mild intellectual disability or developmental disability, assumptions about difficulties learning academic content are set in the identification definitions themselves. What do we want inclusive model to be? Without clear consensus on what inclusive education means and what the model in Ontario refers to, debate around its success is a bit like arguing over who makes the authentic version of an unwritten family recipe. What’s really needed, instead, is to ask: What do we want this model to be? To enact and evaluate change to increase successful outcomes for students, we need to think about what we value in terms of the where, what and how of education, for the approximately 16 per cent of the Ontario student population with special education needs. Students see themselves reflected in their curriculum, their physical surroundings and the broader environment.” Special education policy in Ontario requires boards to make note of their special education “service-delivery model” for students with exceptionalities, within their ministry-reviewed annual special education plans . However, the requirement doesn’t ask boards how services for students relate to fostering inclusion. Inclusion models have evolved Over time, inclusion models in general have evolved . The focus shifted from where students learn (from special education to general education classrooms) to where and how students learn. This change has involved adding specialized and inclusive teaching strategies in general classroom settings. Current models combine a focus on where, how and what students learn. “What” implies robust academic expectations and sufficient support for academic achievement. Ontario decisions about where students learn — termed “educational placement decisions” — are made by the Identification, Placement, and Review Committees . These include at least three members (for example: a school principal, students 16 years or older, a student’s parents and other relevant school staff). Research from my colleagues and me shows that educational placement in general settings has increased over time, but not for all students. Students with behavioural exceptionalities did not see increased placements in inclusive settings. Students identified with developmental disabilities or who are deaf or hard of hearing had some increased placements in general classrooms, but still had the lowest placements there. Researchers have documented the subjective and contextual nature of such decisions. Like other researchers , we also found that external factors , including school board and student age, were significant predictors of educational placement decisions. Read more: Navigating special education labels is complex, and it matters for education equity How students learn: support decisions Ontario’s Learning for All policy promoted general inclusive strategies such as Universal Design for Learning and Differentiated Instruction. But support decisions are made by a student’s educators and recorded and tracked in the student’s Individual Education Plan (IEP). Ontario’s latest audit report and research on teacher training in the province point to problems in teacher education, as well as resources and practices that can negatively influence developing IEPs and ultimately student learning supports. Read more: Children on individual education plans: What parents need to know, and 4 questions they should ask What students learn The Ontario curriculum is designed to describe essential learning expectations for knowledge and skills for all students across the province. Students with special education needs may receive supports accessing the curriculum through educational accommodations. These increase support but don’t change the learning expectation. However, some students with disabilities access the curriculum in a modified format: learning expectations are simplified. Modifications can be helpful to identify learning gaps and provide high-intensity supports. However, there are concerns that this approach is overused, as noted in the Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read inquiry report . Beyond curricular modification, students with exceptionalities may also participate in alternate programs, addressing, for example, life skills. Similar to placement and supports, educational content access is determined on a case-by-case basis for students with special education. For some students, like those with a learning disability, mild intellectual disability or developmental disability, assumptions about difficulties learning academic content are set in the identification definitions themselves. What do we want inclusive model to be? Without clear consensus on what inclusive education means and what the model in Ontario refers to, debate around its success is a bit like arguing over who makes the authentic version of an unwritten family recipe. What’s really needed, instead, is to ask: What do we want this model to be? To enact and evaluate change to increase successful outcomes for students, we need to think about what we value in terms of the where, what and how of education, for the approximately 16 per cent of the Ontario student population with special education needs. articles.title: For better inclusive education that really supports students, we need to consider what we value

articles.content: Editor’s note: This story is part of a series of articles from Canada’s top social sciences and humanities academics in a partnership between the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and The Conversation Canada. Back in 2008, every other week during the school year, my research team (six students in Concordia University’s Design and Computation Arts department as well as two research associates in my lab) and I made the 20-minute drive from Montréal to the Kahnawake Survival School . We’d been invited by Owisokon Lahache, a Kahnawake Mohawk artist and arts teacher. Our goal was to prototype a new model for teaching Indigenous teenagers digital production skills within the context of their community’s history, language and culture. What we learned there changed how I thought about research itself. We spent that fall immersed in storytelling and discussing the importance of those stories to the community. In the winter, we focused on teaching the students tools and techniques for making video games — storyboarding, concept art, modelling, animation and programming. In March, we asked them to use what they had learned to design a video game themselves. We weren’t sure what the students would come up with, and were particularly curious about whether the students would be able to translate oral storytelling into an interactive video game. When we returned to their classroom, we were astounded. Spread across four desks was white butcher paper with a complete game level designed in pencil and clay. The students had taken a monster from one story, a landscape from another and a conflict from a third and remixed them into a new narrative without our guidance. It was then that we realized how excited they had been to be asked to tell their community’s stories in their own way. The students understood video games and had no problem designing one whose world, characters and internal logic were rooted in their own knowledge systems and territory. That experience — a combination of tradition, technology and preparing Indigenous youth for fluency in the digital storytelling tools of the future — became a major driver behind the creation of the Initiative for Indigenous Futures (IIF) . Flipping the research relationship IIF was a partnership of universities and community organizations in Canada, funded by a Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC) Partnership Grant (as well as a Trudeau Fellowship) running from 2015 to 2022. Over seven years, IIF worked with people from numerous communities across Canada, the U.S. and the Pacific, including Kanien’kehá:ka, Cree, Anishinaabe, Diné, Métis, Mi'kmaq, Kānaka Maoli and Māori. We invited experts from many domains — fine arts, design, computer science, history, language — to join us, and we relied on our shared passion to establish methodologies that allowed us to work across communities and disciplines. At its core was a concept called the Indigenous Future Imaginary : the idea that Indigenous Peoples must first imagine the futures we want before we can build our way toward them — that the visions communities hold of their tomorrows shape the work they do today. Developing those imagined futures required spaces for Indigenous communities to dream, cultural grounding to maintain continuity, freedom to speculate creatively and technical capacity to help turn those visions into reality. IIF was designed to provide all four. The partnership model IIF developed was a deliberate departure from how academic research typically works . Often, universities set the questions, communities provide access or data and outcomes circulate within institutions the communities rarely encounter. IIF inverted this. Community members developed their own future imaginaries, with IIF providing support and encouragement, and research questions were developed in response: What are Kanien'kehá:ka values? What does a video game look like when it’s designed to carry them? What creative and technical infrastructure do Indigenous artists need to visualize futures and sustain a practice over time? That inversion took shape through four interconnected pillars: workshops that built technical capacity; residencies supporting artists’ deep engagement with the technology, along with commissions to help populate the future with Indigenous images; symposia and lecture series that circulated these methods more widely; and preservation of digital media artworks for future generations. Skins Workshops on Aboriginal Storytelling in Digital Media , one of IIF’s main initiatives, is now in its 18th year, after 120 workshops reaching more than 1,500 participants across communities from Canada to Hawai'i to Aotearoa to Finland. Another IIF initiative led to Abundant Intelligences , the $28 million international research collaboration exploring how to integrate AI into Indigenous knowledge systems. Collaborations generate grounded outcomes The Initiative for Indigenous Futures model carries lessons well beyond Indigenous research contexts for the scholars who design studies, the institutions that house them and the funders who pay for them. For scholars, investing time in the communities where you’ve built research establishes a foundation of trust that makes it possible to do work that is generative for them and you. Read more: Canada’s first Inuit-led university is coming to Nunavut — here’s why it matters For academic institutions, shared intellectual leadership provides sustained knowledge production where different problems have time to come into view and be addressed. It creates the space for epistemological breadth that enriches our understanding of innovative ways of engaging with our world. For funders, it means that research impact looks different when it is shaped with and for community. Workshops, artworks, games and technical capacity built over years are not soft outputs alongside the “real” academic work. They are the real work. When more communities are given the tools, the space and the institutional trust to imagine their futures on their own terms, the futures we collectively arrive at are richer, more honest and better equipped to hold the full complexity of what it means to live in the world. Jason Edward Lewis receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the Canadian Fund for Innovation, the New Frontiers of Research Fund, the MacArthur Foundation, and the Schmidt Family Foundation.

articles.content: Google recently announced that its AI tools, including Gemini and Gemini Notebook, would be turned off by default for kindergarten to Grade 12 student accounts starting in early 2027. Google Search, its popular search engine, would also be turned off by default. The New York Times reported that Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, said: “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” and that if a school has banned A.I. , “they will not have access to search.” This means schools that want students to simply search on Google will have to accept Google’s AI whether they want it or not. As researchers who study education policy and technology, we see Google’s move as a wake-up call. It exposes how much power one company holds over schools, and why Canadian governments working with school boards, teacher unions and parents need to set the terms for how AI enters classrooms. Setting common regulatory standards at the federal and provincial levels could give schools the collective leverage they currently lack when dealing with trillion-dollar companies like Google . Read more: The release of AI chatbots has harmed teens’ learning and Canada needs to act How did we get here? Google presents the change as giving schools more control amid pushback from child-safety advocates, parents and educators after it switched on Gemini by default in Google Classroom for many K-12 students in August. Google Classroom is an online platform where teachers post assignments and students submit their work. Google has also said AI in its search function will guide students through problems step by step rather than give them quick answers. But guided or not, AI remains built in. Over the past 15 years, Google has become one of the largest providers of digital infrastructure to schools around the world largely by offering its tools for free or at low cost — although researchers highlight hidden costs in the form of data trails left exposed by privacy loopholes . Google’s ‘ecosystem’ Its influence comes not simply from selling individual products to schools, but from embedding schools within an interconnected ecosystem of software applications such as Google Classroom, hardware like Chromebooks and cloud-based services like Google Drive — all increasingly relied upon by schools. About 150 million students and teachers worldwide now use Google Classroom while 60 per cent of all Chromebook purchases are for use in education. This ecosystem approach gives Google immense leverage over schools. Even when offered a “choice,” schools cannot simply switch away from Google overnight. Switching to alternatives involves not only purchasing new software and hardware but also migrating data, retraining teachers and students and disrupting established routines and practices. Google’s decision to tie Search to AI shows how this dependence can become a form of coercion. ‘Pipeline of future users’ Although Google presents its investments in education as altruistic and benign , its commercial interests have always been central to its strategy. Internal company documents, filed in a U.S. lawsuit against Google and other social media companies, describe Google’s work in schools as building a “pipeline of future users.” A Google spokesperson said the documents “mischaracterize our work.” Read more: We street-proof our kids. Why aren’t we data-proofing them? Google Search, the company’s biggest revenue-generating business , lies at the core of that pipeline. As AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude gain popularity as alternatives to traditional internet search , they threaten not only Google’s current user base but also its future one. A generation that learns to access information online without “Googling” as its primary gateway is what Google wants to prevent. Seen from this lens, it’s no surprise Google isn’t letting schools search on Google without AI features embedded in one form or another. Who is setting the rules? This conundrum facing schools raises a central question: who sets the direction and conditions for AI in K-12 education? The Council of Ontario Directors of Education’s 2026 “AI in Education” resource cautions that students and staff are already using AI “in the absence of guidance.” Read more: Should AI chatbots simulate care for students? Alberta teachers say no For the 2026-27 school year, the Ontario education ministry required “Cyber Safety and Artificial Intelligence” to be one of four mandatory topics on teachers’ professional activity days, which includes getting familiar with AI tools. British Columbia has published a set of considerations to help school districts select AI tools. But it sets no rules of its own, leaving individual districts to make their own decisions. This approach assumes districts have meaningful choices. But Google sets the same terms for all schools, and changes them when it chooses. At the federal level, the emphasis has been more on AI adoption. In September, the federal government launched a $13-million National AI Literacy Initiative , in partnership with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, that includes free, self-paced modules that show K-12 educators how to integrate AI into curriculum, assessment and teaching. The Canadian Teachers’ Federation has warned that the initiative puts “adoption before safety,” encouraging teachers to bring AI into classrooms before its safety and educational benefits can be established. Regulatory standards needed Google’s ultimatum shows why a human-centred approach to AI in education must begin with a fundamental question: Who gets to decide whether and how AI enters classrooms? Such an approach prioritizes students’ needs, rights and learning and teachers’ professional judgment over technology companies’ commercial interests. UNESCO’s guidance on generative AI in education points in this direction, setting out distinct responsibilities for governments, AI providers and users. Researchers have argued AI should be regulated through a developmental lens before it enters K-12 classrooms, and there is already evidence of why such safeguards are warranted. Read more: School board social media lawsuits: For too long we’ve sought individual solutions to a collective problem In July 2026, Common Sense Media gave the AI features in Google Search its lowest possible rating, “ unacceptable risk ,” after finding that they completed students’ homework assignments and failed to respond appropriately to children in crisis. Google disputed the findings , saying the testing relied on “a narrow set of ambiguous and contrived queries.” Questions about whether these tools are safe for children shouldn’t be settled by school boards alone. Setting joint standards allows school boards to weigh the educational value of AI against other pressing priorities, rather than treating its adoption as inevitable in already underfunded education systems . Rajender Singh is a Senior Policy Analyst at The Dais, a university based think tank at Toronto Metropolitan University, whose work includes technology and K-12 education. Melody Viczko and Yadira Lizama Mué do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Google’s AI ultimatum exposes the risks of schools’ dependence on Big Tech

articles.content: There is very little on which the National Post and the Toronto Star can agree in this age of polarization. As bastions of the right and the left in Canadian media, they squabble over the environment, women’s rights and race. But on one thing they seem to agree: masculinity is in crisis. The National Post complains that “plenty of commentators claim the manosphere is luring boys into monstrous ideas.” The Toronto Star argues that “young men don’t benefit from what the right is selling them.” The two newspapers reach opposite conclusions, but they start from the same premise: that there is a normative masculinity, that it is now in crisis and that their readers share an understanding of what “crisis” means. That shared understanding is rarely examined. Media portrayals of the “crisis of masculinity” seldom ask what is actually meant when the words “crisis” and “masculinity” are invoked. Asking those questions reveals two things: when, and for whom, the crisis label gets applied is heavily unequal. And the “masculinity” said to be in crisis is often a very specific, very white kind of masculinity. What is a crisis? “Crisis” comes from the Greek krinō , which meant merely a decisive moment and the reaching of a verdict about said moment. Around the 18th century, as historian and theorist Reinhart Koselleck notes , crisis came to be associated with a new kind of temporality: no longer just the moment of decision, but the time after it — the end of the era in which the decision was made. Any crisis, then, contains a tacit agreement between whoever declares it — a politician, an advocate, a newspaper — and the people being told about it. Both must accept that there is a state of normalcy against which the crisis is defined. But as anthropologist Janet Roitman points out , what is and is not normative is socially constructed. There is no empirical state of “crisis” or “non-crisis.” A crisis is perhaps best understood, then, as a social label applied to a series of failures of category, in this case gender. In its current usage, a crisis is a failure mediated through political and ideological frameworks . It becomes a crisis when someone says it is, and when the failure is taken as a symptom of a wider problem. Crisis as a political tool The right’s embrace of crisis rhetoric has been studied by the likes of political scientist Benjamin Moffitt. In his 2015 paper “How to Perform Crisis: A Model for Understanding the Key Role of Crisis in Contemporary Populism,” he describes “crisis” as an “ill-defined” yet politically salient category. It’s one that far-right populists such as Geert Wilders, leader of the Netherlands’ Party for Freedom , and Australia’s Pauline Hanson, leader of the One Nation party , mobilize to rally their bases. The political right has raised the profile of the “crisis of masculinity” over the past decade, and the frame has travelled. In a November 2025 interview on CNN’s State of the Union , California Gov. Gavin Newsom lamented that, in his view, Democrats had ceded ground on the “crisis of masculinity” by not taking the epidemic of male suicide seriously . When a Democratic governor adopts the phrase, it is no longer only a right-wing talking point. Which men? The “crisis of masculinity” usually refers to a wide range of problems, but it rarely specifies the kind of man on whom those problems fall. Men do die by suicide at higher rates than women in Canada (roughly three times the rate) . But those rates are far from even among men. Among Inuit in Nunavut, for example, suicide occurs at about 10 times the rate in the rest of Canada , and young men are at highest risk . Inuit have named this a crisis themselves. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami’s 2016 National Inuit Suicide Prevention Strategy frames suicide among Inuit as a preventable public health crisis that demands a systemic response. Indigenous men are also more likely than anyone else in Canada to be killed . In 2020, police reported 201 Indigenous homicide victims; 163 of them were men . That year, the homicide rate for Indigenous men was almost eight times the rate for non-Indigenous men. Government agencies have documented this harm. Yet it rarely appears when commentators talk about “the crisis of masculinity.” The people closest to the harm name the crisis long before those with power treat it as one. What becomes clear, then, is that this “crisis” is often about the grievances of white men. Read more: International Men’s Day: Young men are struggling — but not all men are struggling equally Words have meaning In the discourse around the “crisis of masculinity,” the word “masculinity” functions as a shorthand for a kind of white masculinity that has historically been seen as above gendered and racialized crises expected to befall other groups of men. The suicide rate among young Inuit men is intolerably high. Yet that is not treated with anything like the urgency and panic that greets the “crisis” of white masculinity. The National Post and the Toronto Star may never agree on what men need. But if they agree that men are in crisis, the next question needs to be: which men? W. Trent Atkinson does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

Around the 18th century, as historian and theorist Reinhart Koselleck notes , crisis came to be associated with a new kind of temporality: no longer just the moment of decision, but the time after it — the end of the era in which the decision was made. Any crisis, then, contains a tacit agreement between whoever declares it — a politician, an advocate, a newspaper — and the people being told about it. Both must accept that there is a state of normalcy against which the crisis is defined. But as anthropologist Janet Roitman points out , what is and is not normative is socially constructed. There is no empirical state of “crisis” or “non-crisis.” A crisis is perhaps best understood, then, as a social label applied to a series of failures of category, in this case gender. In its current usage, a crisis is a failure mediated through political and ideological frameworks . It becomes a crisis when someone says it is, and when the failure is taken as a symptom of a wider problem. Crisis as a political tool The right’s embrace of crisis rhetoric has been studied by the likes of political scientist Benjamin Moffitt. In his 2015 paper “How to Perform Crisis: A Model for Understanding the Key Role of Crisis in Contemporary Populism,” he describes “crisis” as an “ill-defined” yet politically salient category. It’s one that far-right populists such as Geert Wilders, leader of the Netherlands’ Party for Freedom , and Australia’s Pauline Hanson, leader of the One Nation party , mobilize to rally their bases. The political right has raised the profile of the “crisis of masculinity” over the past decade, and the frame has travelled. In a November 2025 interview on CNN’s State of the Union , California Gov. Gavin Newsom lamented that, in his view, Democrats had ceded ground on the “crisis of masculinity” by not taking the epidemic of male suicide seriously . When a Democratic governor adopts the phrase, it is no longer only a right-wing talking point. Which men? The “crisis of masculinity” usually refers to a wide range of problems, but it rarely specifies the kind of man on whom those problems fall. Men do die by suicide at higher rates than women in Canada (roughly three times the rate) . But those rates are far from even among men. Among Inuit in Nunavut, for example, suicide occurs at about 10 times the rate in the rest of Canada , and young men are at highest risk . Inuit have named this a crisis themselves. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami’s 2016 National Inuit Suicide Prevention Strategy frames suicide among Inuit as a preventable public health crisis that demands a systemic response. Indigenous men are also more likely than anyone else in Canada to be killed . In 2020, police reported 201 Indigenous homicide victims; 163 of them were men . That year, the homicide rate for Indigenous men was almost eight times the rate for non-Indigenous men. Government agencies have documented this harm. Yet it rarely appears when commentators talk about “the crisis of masculinity.” The people closest to the harm name the crisis long before those with power treat it as one. What becomes clear, then, is that this “crisis” is often about the grievances of white men. Read more: International Men’s Day: Young men are struggling — but not all men are struggling equally Words have meaning In the discourse around the “crisis of masculinity,” the word “masculinity” functions as a shorthand for a kind of white masculinity that has historically been seen as above gendered and racialized crises expected to befall other groups of men. The suicide rate among young Inuit men is intolerably high. Yet that is not treated with anything like the urgency and panic that greets the “crisis” of white masculinity. The National Post and the Toronto Star may never agree on what men need. But if they agree that men are in crisis, the next question needs to be: which men? W.
