articles.content: Tokyo then, St. John's now? A giant squid attacks a bait squid off the coast of Tokyo in 2006. (Tsunemi Kubodera/National Science Museum of Japan) , CC BY When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below , about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport , I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!” First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work , the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett). Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence. Unveiling the giant squid One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey , who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony. Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London. Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich , joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid. Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches. Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles. The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals. Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety. The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust. This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!) I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis. But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice. As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction. Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures. He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it. I certainly enjoyed watching Below , not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history. The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say). It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s. It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony , and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series. Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged Stoking interest in the ocean I am not a particular fan of the horror genre, though I recognize its nod to productions from decades earlier when creatures emerged from the ocean depths to wreak havoc on an unsuspecting humanity (think Godzilla , Jaws , and Orca ). Though the genre isn’t for everyone, most people I asked said they enjoyed the series, and particularly the Newfoundland ambience. I also applaud the Below team for communicating the complexity of the ocean, and their efforts to capture the imagination and interest of the public with its many unknowns. The series also underscored the ongoing potential for ocean exploration. Scientists discover thousands of new marine species every year and could discover many more if there were more of us. Many of these discoveries come from the deep sea , where giant squid spend most of their time. Most new marine species are small animals, but, as scientists sample more ocean, a surprise discovery occasionally emerges not unlike the giant squid in Below . Perhaps given Below ’s success ( the No. 1 ranked show in Canada on Netflix the week after its release , with an 87 per cent Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes ), Hollywood might see some potential in telling exciting stories that bring the ocean into our living rooms. That focus could inspire a new generation of scientists. I can’t help thinking that watching Jaws and Orca when I was an impressionable teen helped to push my career interests towards the ocean, where my ancestors had also earned their living. Paul Snelgrove receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Council of Canada and the Canada First Research Excellence Fund.

Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London. Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich , joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid. Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches. Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles. The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals. Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety. The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust. This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!) I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis. But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice. As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction. Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures. He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it. I certainly enjoyed watching Below , not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history. The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say). It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s. It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony , and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series. Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged Stoking interest in the ocean I am not a particular fan of the horror genre, though I recognize its nod to productions from decades earlier when creatures emerged from the ocean depths to wreak havoc on an unsuspecting humanity (think Godzilla , Jaws , and Orca ). Though the genre isn’t for everyone, most people I asked said they enjoyed the series, and particularly the Newfoundland ambience. I also applaud the Below team for communicating the complexity of the ocean, and their efforts to capture the imagination and interest of the public with its many unknowns. The series also underscored the ongoing potential for ocean exploration. Scientists discover thousands of new marine species every year and could discover many more if there were more of us. Many of these discoveries come from the deep sea , where giant squid spend most of their time. Most new marine species are small animals, but, as scientists sample more ocean, a surprise discovery occasionally emerges not unlike the giant squid in Below . Perhaps given Below ’s success ( the No. 1 ranked show in Canada on Netflix the week after its release , with an 87 per cent Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes ), Hollywood might see some potential in telling exciting stories that bring the ocean into our living rooms. That focus could inspire a new generation of scientists. I can’t help thinking that watching Jaws and Orca when I was an impressionable teen helped to push my career interests towards the ocean, where my ancestors had also earned their living. Paul Snelgrove receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Council of Canada and the Canada First Research Excellence Fund.
articles.title: What lurks ‘Below’ Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show

articles.content: Elizabeth Holmes is questioned by Nathan Fielder in 'You Can See Everything.' (A24) This story contains a spoiler about ‘You Can See Everything .’ Canadian comedian Nathan Fielder’s runaway-hit documentary You Can See Everything reintroduces audiences to Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud in 2022 . Holmes maintains she is innocent . Through Fielder’s lens, the film prompts us to question her conduct anew by exploring the meaning of acting, drama, truth, lies and fiction. In the film, Holmes objects to a quote of hers reported by the New York Times . According to the Times , Holmes said of actors portraying her: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” In Fielder’s documentary, Holmes’s husband reads the quote and says it doesn’t sound like something she would say . He suggests Holmes said instead: “They’re playing a character they created,” and she agrees. Partly through the film’s interviews with Holmes and her husband, as well as commentary by Fielder, viewers are led to wonder: Has she been playing a character she created, intended to deceive others? Is she now playing a role? Does she even know? Playing a role If Holmes is deliberately playing a role, we are inclined to condemn her as a fraudulent deceiver, well-deserving of her punishment; if not, we may be more inclined to see her sympathetically — flawed, caught up in a scheme largely wrought by others. ‘You Can See Everything’ trailer. It might seem that, because each person knows what they’re doing, they’re the authority on whether they are playing a role. But Fielder’s film, and his previous work that straddles the line between awkward comedy and social inquiry , challenges where the boundaries lie. In his HBO docuseries The Rehearsal , Fielder plays himself as a director helping people prepare for difficult situations by staging elaborate rehearsals of how they might unfold . The series leads the audience to question the relationship between the rehearsals and the real situation they mean to influence. Actions, imitations One way to think about this is by examining the difference between doing things and acting as though we’re doing them — for the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, the difference between an action and an imitation. To frame this issue more carefully, we can turn to a distinction Aristotle drew between “action” and “production.” For Aristotle, the arts are particular kinds of know-how. A shoemaker, for instance, knows how to produce shoes. Drama, writes Aristotle, knows how to produce the imitation ( mimēsis ) of actions . The actor’s aim is to produce a compelling imitation of someone, say, making a shoe. That imitated action is the product of the art. When done well, the audience is convinced they have seen someone do the action, perhaps briefly forgetting it was only an imitation. Often, an actor playing a shoemaker does not go so far as to make a shoe. But what if they do? ‘The Fielder Method’ The fourth episode of The Rehearsal , “The Fielder Method,” sees Fielder describe a method to train people to perform on his show. Fielder invites actors to shadow a person, called their “primary,” to learn how to imitate them in the rehearsals. He goes so far as to have them work the job of their primary or even move into a similar living arrangement. Following this method, it very well may be the case that an actor playing a shoemaker makes a real shoe. “The Fielder Method” shows that the distinction between “imitated action” and “genuine action” is porous. An audience, actor can get lost An effective imitation convinces audiences, temporarily, that we are witnessing the action, and we respond to it, at least in part, as a doing of that action. The audience can get lost in whether what they are seeing is an action or its imitation. An effective imitation, then, can be a powerful tool in the hands of someone intent on deception. Yet, as Fielder’s work also suggests, the actor can get caught up in their role. In The Rehearsal (“Pretend Daddy”), Fielder (playing himself) is rehearsing parenting a six-year old child. The child actor playing his child becomes attached to Fielder, calling him “daddy.” Fielder himself seemingly has real feelings for the child actor. If what an actor does as an imitation coincides with the actual deed so precisely that its outcome is indistinguishable from the real thing, its status hangs on what comes next: The actor’s stepping out of character and returning to “real life.” But what if the actor doesn’t step out of character? What if they leave “real life” behind? In The Rehearsal , Fielder becomes so committed to understanding pilots that he becomes one, flying a Boeing 737 from takeoff to landing. Is it plausible that Holmes, too, began intent on deception, playing a brilliant, Steve Jobs-like CEO, but then became lost in the role, increasingly unable to acknowledge distance between herself and the character she created? Or is this explanation a perfect hiding place to deny responsibility? ‘Why would I deceive you?’ A viral scene where Holmes asks Fielder, “Why would I deceive you?” is astonishing because there is such a clear reason for Holmes to deceive Fielder. In the film, partly through Fielder’s dialogue with actor Amanda Seyfried , who played Holmes in a miniseries , the film deals with how to understand Holmes. Their dialogue is interspersed with newly created scenes of Seyfried playing Holmes in Fielder’s documentary to study her, using the technique developed in The Rehearsal . One explanation could be that Holmes believes herself, or has become lost in her role. This would not excuse her crimes. But it might suggest that understanding her properly requires us to think about the role of imitation and art in our lives, just as Fielder’s works challenge us to do. On the other hand, what exactly have we seen? Commentators have raised ethical concerns around how Fielder’s relationship to his subject shapes what we do and importantly don’t see (such as the impacts of Holmes’s fraud) — or genre questions , including whether it really should be called a documentary. Read more: Can you see everything? Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes face off in You Can See Everything A compelling imitation, Aristotle tells us , is delightful because we love to learn, and imitation teaches us. This may be why scores of audiences are going to cinemas to watch an almost three-hour-long documentary . Drama can be deployed for deception, but as both Aristotle and Fielder show us, it can also be an essential vehicle for questioning our assumptions about reality. John Robert Hacker-Wright does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Imagine you are sitting on a train, moving at a constant speed. The blinds are drawn so you can’t tell you are moving. A light bulb hangs on a chain in the centre of the car. When someone turns it on, your human eye perceives the whole carriage lighting up. What actually happens is that light first reaches the two sides of the car simultaneously. A moment later, the light reaches the front and back of the car, again simultaneously. The light has travelled at the exact same speed in all four directions. Albert Einstein wondered how this situation would be described from the perspective of someone outside the train who was not moving with the car. For a drone hovering over the train, for example, the light still reaches the two sides simultaneously but the back of the car lights up before the front. This is because the train is moving forward, so in the moment it takes the light to travel to the front and back of the car, the back has moved closer to the light source and the front has moved further away. This phenomenon, discovered by Einstein in 1905 , is called the “relativity of simultaneity.” Physicist Brian Greene explains the concept of the relativity of simultaneity (World Science Festival). On the basis of this phenomenon, scientists have argued that in reality there is no objective “now” and that time does not truly pass. Some have even suggested that the apparent passage of time may be psychological . Modern cosmological observations, however, suggest that time is more than a mere illusion. The illusion of now Einstein himself declared time to be an illusion. On the passing of his friend and fellow physicist, Michele Besso, he wrote: “Now he has departed from this strange world a little ahead of me. That means nothing. People like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion .” Along with Einstein, physicists and philosophers have often used relativity to argue there is no such thing as true simultaneity. For example, if you could say that a star several hundred light-years away is exploding “right now,” you could also stand up and walk away from it and just as well conclude that it won’t explode for another minute or so. By extension, if there is no objective now, and if all relative “nows” are on equal footing, then perhaps reality encompasses all of “ spacetime ” — every event that ever happens anywhere across the universe throughout all of eternity. Perhaps, as Einstein said, time really is nothing but a stubbornly persistent illusion. From the perspective of modern cosmology, however, it seems that an objective “now” does exist. Is the train really moving? It is tempting to say that the drone hovering in a fixed place above the train in our scenario is “at rest” and that the train is “really moving.” But we know the Earth is rapidly spinning and orbiting the Sun, which is orbiting the Milky Way, which is moving relative to nearby galaxies and so on. A composite image of the central region of our of the Milky Way galaxy using images from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, Spitzer Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/CXC/STScI) Therefore, neither drone nor train can be defined as “the one that’s moving” or “the one at rest” in any absolute sense. We could define either as an equally valid relative state of rest. On the other hand, if there was an absolute state of rest and an objectively well-defined “now,” we would require a concrete scientific measurement showing that the associated space has always persisted as such, along with a way to measure velocity through it from anywhere in the universe at any time. That would make the one state of rest objectively well-defined relative to all others. Such a space could then be said to “exist” in the usual sense of the word, with Earth and all of us existing in it, and it would provide consistent definitions of “now” and of “motion.” The cosmic now Cosmology delivers this. We have already made the required measurements using the cosmic microwave background (CMB) — the cooled remains of the first light released after the Big Bang. The CMB reveals that our universe — the three-dimensional expanding space where we live and evolve — has existed for approximately 13.8 billion years. It also shows the universe to have expanded by an integrated factor of about 1,100 since it formed; and that our solar system is moving through it with a velocity of 369.82 kilometres per second towards the Crater constellation . Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. (Wikimedia) The integrated expansion of space throughout cosmic time has been so precise in every direction we look that across the sky we can measure “ anisotropies ” that were imprinted on the CMB at the time it was formed. These are tiny differences in the CMB’s temperature from one direction to another, of about one part in 100,000, which map the slightly denser and slightly thinner regions of the early universe. It would be impossible to see this if space were not objectively defined and expansion had been different here and there. This means that Einstein’s relativity of simultaneity still applies to local phenomena as a matter of relative perspective: neither the train nor the drone gets to say they are the one that is truly at rest, and both frames of reference can be used to describe reality, just as Einstein found. However, contrary to his belief, time is more than a mere illusion. The implication from modern cosmology is that the universe exists, and events happen all across space in the course of cosmic time. These events may be described as synchronous or not, depending on one’s motion through the universe, although there is in reality one cosmic time and an objective measure of simultaneity. Daryl Janzen does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Canadians aged 65 and older want to decide where they live and most prefer that place to be their current home . The concept of an older adult aging in the place of their choosing emphasizes that preference. Preference, however, does not guarantee that aging in that place will be possible. Feasibility depends on an older person’s circumstances and supports available where they live. John Amagoalik’s story illustrates the gap between preference and possibility when it comes to aging in place of choice. A lifelong advocate for Inuit self-determination and one of the key figures behind the creation of Nunavut , Amagoalik recently spent 16 months in an assisted-living facility in Ottawa after an infection resulted in the amputation of part of his leg. Being more than 2,000 kilometres from Iqaluit, Amagoalik told the CBC, “The worst part was the loneliness.” Friends eventually helped arrange the housing and care that has allowed him to return to his home for now. Although Amagoalik’s circumstances are particular to Nunavut, where some elders must leave the territory to access specialized services not available closer to home , his story raises a question relevant across Canada: What does it mean to say older persons have a choice about where they age if the supports they need are not available where they want to live? What determines where people age As occupational therapists and rehabilitation scientists , our research explores how engagement in everyday activities contributes to health and well-being in later life. Our work has led us to recognize that where people age is shaped not only by their preferences but also by their circumstances and supports around them. For us, this research is also personal. Our mothers continue to live independently, and both chose to move closer to family. Like many with aging parents, we think about what will allow them to continue doing so if their health, mobility or circumstances change. Having a choice about where one lives as one grows older requires realistic options. Rural communities can offer strong social connections and a sense of belonging, but as needs change, limited access to transportation, affordable and accessible housing, and other health and social services may constrain people’s ability to remain in the place they call home. Rural aging and mobility Research on rural aging has described a related tension between “aging in place” and being “stuck in place .” Remaining somewhere does not necessarily mean an older person had a meaningful choice to do so. Transportation provides a good example. Our research with older persons living in rural areas and small towns around Hamilton, Ont., identified considerable reliance on personal vehicles . If few alternatives exist, losing the ability to drive can mean losing access not only to medical appointments and groceries, but also to activities and relationships outside the home. Mobility, after all, is about much more than getting from one place to another. Being able to get around allows us to see friends and family, volunteer, exercise or simply participate in everyday activities that make life meaningful. However, what happens when driving is no longer possible and there is no realistic alternative? If managing your current home becomes difficult, is there help or a suitable and affordable option nearby? Can needed services be accessed without leaving your community? These questions also make us think differently about risk. Risk and what matters Families and health professionals understandably worry about falls , driving safety or whether an older adult can live at home alone . While those risks matter, our research has identified that focusing too much on physical safety can sometimes overshadow what older people themselves value when decisions are being made about where and how they will live. Stopping driving may reduce one kind of risk while increasing risks of isolation and loss of meaningful activities . Moving somewhere with more services may make some aspects of life easier or safer but moving away from neighbours, relationships and a place we call home has consequences for well-being. A home that no longer meets an older person’s needs can carry risk, but so can leaving it. Supporting real choice Planning ahead for mobility changes matters but so do housing, relationships, finances and ensuring support is available. However, people cannot plan around options that do not exist. Supporting real choice about aging in place also means asking: Can older community residents get where they need and want to go? Are housing, health and social supports accessible where people live? When those supports are not available, who fills the gaps? Families, friends and neighbours provide extraordinary support and can expand an older person’s choices but should not be the only infrastructure upon which aging at home depends . Aging in a place of choice cannot simply mean asking older people where they want to live. Communities and governments must ensure people have meaningful and realistic options as their health, mobility and circumstances change. Choice only means something when there are real options. articles.description: Canadians aged 65 and older want to decide where they live and most prefer that place to be their current home . The concept of an older adult aging in the place of their choosing emphasizes that preference. Preference, however, does not guarantee that aging in that place will be possible. Feasibility depends on an older person’s circumstances and supports available where they live. John Amagoalik’s story illustrates the gap between preference and possibility when it comes to aging in place of choice. A lifelong advocate for Inuit self-determination and one of the key figures behind the creation of Nunavut , Amagoalik recently spent 16 months in an assisted-living facility in Ottawa after an infection resulted in the amputation of part of his leg. Being more than 2,000 kilometres from Iqaluit, Amagoalik told the CBC, “The worst part was the loneliness.” Friends eventually helped arrange the housing and care that has allowed him to return to his home for now. Although Amagoalik’s circumstances are particular to Nunavut, where some elders must leave the territory to access specialized services not available closer to home , his story raises a question relevant across Canada: What does it mean to say older persons have a choice about where they age if the supports they need are not available where they want to live? What determines where people age As occupational therapists and rehabilitation scientists , our research explores how engagement in everyday activities contributes to health and well-being in later life. Our work has led us to recognize that where people age is shaped not only by their preferences but also by their circumstances and supports around them. For us, this research is also personal. Our mothers continue to live independently, and both chose to move closer to family. Like many with aging parents, we think about what will allow them to continue doing so if their health, mobility or circumstances change. Having a choice about where one lives as one grows older requires realistic options. Rural communities can offer strong social connections and a sense of belonging, but as needs change, limited access to transportation, affordable and accessible housing, and other health and social services may constrain people’s ability to remain in the place they call home. Rural aging and mobility Research on rural aging has described a related tension between “aging in place” and being “stuck in place .” Remaining somewhere does not necessarily mean an older person had a meaningful choice to do so. Transportation provides a good example. Our research with older persons living in rural areas and small towns around Hamilton, Ont., identified considerable reliance on personal vehicles . If few alternatives exist, losing the ability to drive can mean losing access not only to medical appointments and groceries, but also to activities and relationships outside the home. Mobility, after all, is about much more than getting from one place to another. Being able to get around allows us to see friends and family, volunteer, exercise or simply participate in everyday activities that make life meaningful. However, what happens when driving is no longer possible and there is no realistic alternative? If managing your current home becomes difficult, is there help or a suitable and affordable option nearby? Can needed services be accessed without leaving your community? These questions also make us think differently about risk. Risk and what matters Families and health professionals understandably worry about falls , driving safety or whether an older adult can live at home alone . While those risks matter, our research has identified that focusing too much on physical safety can sometimes overshadow what older people themselves value when decisions are being made about where and how they will live. Stopping driving may reduce one kind of risk while increasing risks of isolation and loss of meaningful activities . Moving somewhere with more services may make some aspects of life easier or safer but moving away from neighbours, relationships and a place we call home has consequences for well-being. A home that no longer meets an older person’s needs can carry risk, but so can leaving it. Supporting real choice Planning ahead for mobility changes matters but so do housing, relationships, finances and ensuring support is available. However, people cannot plan around options that do not exist. Supporting real choice about aging in place also means asking: Can older community residents get where they need and want to go? Are housing, health and social supports accessible where people live? When those supports are not available, who fills the gaps? Families, friends and neighbours provide extraordinary support and can expand an older person’s choices but should not be the only infrastructure upon which aging at home depends . Aging in a place of choice cannot simply mean asking older people where they want to live. Communities and governments must ensure people have meaningful and realistic options as their health, mobility and circumstances change. Choice only means something when there are real options. articles.content: Open any news feed from the past few months, and the disasters arrive in a stream: smoke reaching dangerous levels throughout Canada and flash floods in Ottawa , Montréal and Toronto ; heat and drought arriving together on every continent. Driven by climate change, these events are happening more often, and rather than remaining isolated, they cause cascading, interrelated effects. Now enter the “super” or even “Godzilla” El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific. This phenomenon changes weather patterns globally, potentially bringing more extreme heat, drought and flooding. Although it’s a natural climate phenomenon, scientists are concerned about the unprecedented rate of surface warming. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has declared a greater than 83 per cent probability of strong to very strong El Niño conditions during January to March 2027 . Historical precedents are sobering, with major El Niño events of 1982-83 , 1997-98 and 2015-16 leading to extreme flooding in some regions, severe drought in others, and widespread disruption to ecosystems and economies . Now imagine if hospitals were overrun with respiratory events due to wildfire smoke, migraines, heatstroke and delirium. At the same time, the electricity grid could go down due to overwhelming demand from the use of air conditioning systems. If that scenario sounds plausible, it’s because every element has already happened in Canada, just not all at once. We call these scenarios polycrises, to represent multiple connected crises occurring simultaneously. We’ve seen these before, such as the 2013 Calgary floods , the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and the 2023 Northwest Territories wildfires that required evacuation. The toll of polycrisis on health care The health-care system deserves special consideration when preparing for polycrises. Canada’s health-care system is over capacity on a normal day, with now-familiar hallway medicine, long wait times, surgical delays, understaffing and insufficient primary and long-term care. Canadian access to care ranked ninth of 10 peer countries in a 2025 study , above only the United States. Now imagine adding severe wildfire smoke, a flood causing energy outages and a new viral illness. It’s easy to imagine health-care access and quality declining. Health care suffers at the centre of polycrises. Wildfire smoke has contributed to 1,900 premature deaths annually and $18 billion in costs in Canada. Evidence shows that smoke increases all-cause mortality and causes exacerbations of cardiovascular disease, respiratory conditions , neurologic diseases like multiple sclerosis and migraines . It can trigger stroke and delirium, affect fetal health and has been associated with developing dementia . During the 2023 wildfires, Ontario asthma-related emergency visits increased by 23.6 per cent . Floods disrupt transportation, supplies and patient discharge, while evacuations overwhelm communities, like when 20,000 Northwest Territories residents fled to Alberta in 2023. Supply-chain interruptions threaten access to medications and medical equipment, as seen during COVID-19. These crises disproportionately affect underhoused individuals , people with disabilities, lower-income households and Indigenous communities . Energy implications A strong El Niño can put the entire energy system under strain, just when the health system is most vulnerable. The effects begin months earlier. Milder winters, altered precipitation and reduced mountain snowpack diminish spring runoff and hydroelectric inflows, leaving reservoirs with less stored energy as summer demand peaks arrive. It can also influence the likelihood of extreme summer heat, which often coincides with periods of low wind output. In June 2026, Europe experienced a heat dome accompanied by a wind drought , reducing wind generation just as soaring temperatures drove up electricity demand for cooling. In extreme heat, solar power has lower capacity – known as derating – losing roughly 0.4 per cent for every degree above 25°C , and dims further under wildfire smoke. Gas turbines also lose capacity to hot-air derating on the hottest afternoons. As with the broader polycrisis, the primary issue is convergence. Demand rises precisely when many supply sources are constrained, leaving the grid with less room to absorb the next shock. The shared patient Energy poverty is where the energy system and health system share a patient. While hospitals have backup power and contingency plans, the greatest risks lie in the community. The households least able to afford cooling, air filtration or backup power are the same populations over-represented in heat and smoke morbidity. British Columbia’s 2021 heat dome led to more than 619 deaths, primarily among the elderly and those who lived in under-resourced communities . The heat dome that fills emergency departments with heatstroke and delirium is the same weather system derating the gas turbines that power hospital wards. The smoke triggering asthma exacerbations also reduces the solar output flowing into the grid. The insulin requiring refrigeration, the elevators in seniors’ residences and the oxygen concentrators in patients’ homes all depend on electricity precisely when demand is greatest. This is the defining property of a polycrisis: interconnected failures that neither the energy system nor the health-care system can prepare for alone. What resilience looks like The encouraging part is that the two systems share their defences as surely as they share their failures. Storage, demand flexibility, interties (transmission links that let grids share electricity), backup power at critical facilities and cooling centres with assured power: every investment that hardens the grid against El Niño-pattern stress also protects health outcomes. One system’s resilience budget is the other’s prevention budget. Energy-affordability support is preventive medicine delivered through a utility bill. The El Niño forecast’s real value is lead time. We must act on this warning and secure backup power, fund cooling centres, bolster critical supply chains and identify patients whose health depends on the grid. The time to prepare for a polycrisis is before the emergency is at our doorstep. This story was co-authored by Luke Killam, co-founder and CEO of GreenKey Energy, an independent energy consultancy. The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Right now, Leonard Cohen is on many of his fans’ minds. The Canadian poet, novelist and singer-songwriter died Nov. 7, 2016, just one day before United States President Donald Trump was first elected . Ten years later, as the Democrat “blue wave” hopes to close the bracket on a president who once memed himself as Jesus personified , Cohen’s legacy has become effortlessly epic — even biblical — in quite a different way. Tribute gatherings Tribute gatherings for the singer abound. Cohen was the subject of a sold-out event at the Toronto International Festival of Authors at the end of October. Adam Cohen’s family tour, which began in Canada this month and reaches Europe in winter 2027, pairs his father’s music with archival photos and film . Ottawa’s Gladstone Theatre advertised their “Ten Years Gone” commemoration with a question quite suggestive to people like me who study the evolution of sacred texts: “What would Cohen say today?” Cohen’s ‘contemporary psalms’ As an answer, I highlight an under-celebrated part of Cohen’s poetry and song. As I detail in my 2023 book Prophets of Love: The Unlikely Kinship of Leonard Cohen and the Apostle Paul , all of Cohen’s work is infused with biblical allusions. But some of Cohen’s work does more than echo biblical themes. It takes on biblical format, in the tradition of poetic prayer known in Hebrew as tehillim . Tehillim, or Psalms, inform the Jewish liturgical tradition of addressing God directly, not only in praise, but also in lament, desperation and challenge . This is most explicit in what publisher McClelland and Stewart called Cohen’s “contemporary psalms” in his Book of Mercy . In 1984, as Cohen turned 50, his life provided the material for the 50 psalms of lament, complaint, joy, doubt, adoration and desperation that made up this poetry collection. Like the biblical Psalms, these short poems are numbered rather than titled. Cohen described the collection as “meant for people like myself who could use it, at a particular time,” as “a book of prayer.” Many interpreters continue to analyze this collection as Tehillim . Writing liturgy Although modest about himself in public, Cohen never lacked ambition for his poetry. Rabbi Mordecai Finley , who has read Cohen’s poems aloud for High Holy Days, recalls Cohen confiding that he felt he was always writing not just poetry, but liturgy. Ben Sales points out that Cohen’s song “If It Be Your Will” echoes the Friday evening prayer service welcoming Shabbat, and “Who By Fire” is a nearly word-for-word arrangement of the High Holiday prayer, the “Unetaneh Tokef .” Cohen’s “ Anthem ,” with its famous line “that’s how the light gets in,” inspires ponderings from both Christians and Jews . And “ Hallelujah ,” — a biblical term heard in church services — is a star example of a Cohen song as religious anthem, despite its references to surprisingly carnal biblical texts . I believe Cohen’s grappling with the divine, whether overt, or nestled within his sensual poetry, might prove to be his most enduring memorial. Multiple traditions and levels Cohen biographer and author Harry Freedman reports that Cohen studied in India, referenced the Kabbalah frequently and knew the lore of the Christian Desert Mothers and Fathers . Both Kabbalah and early Christian ascetics blur the boundaries between the erotic and the divine. Cohen’s way of addressing the sensual and the spiritual simultaneously allows the same song to reach different people — or reach the same person at different times. He could also speak from multiple traditions. Cohen was an ordained Rinzai Zen monk , the grandson of a famous rabbi and Talmud scholar. As an impressionable child he went to mass with his Irish nanny in Montréal, a city of churches. In I’m Your Man , music journalist Sylvie Simmons chronicles how Cohen was a deeply knowledgeable Jew who moved comfortably between the Torah, Talmud, Tao Te Ching, Sufi mysticism and the New Testament. No religious tourist Fewer Canadians remember the literary critic Northrop Frye than know Cohen. But the poet turned out to be the perfect example of the professor’s point: the educated imagination lives and breathes the vocabulary of the sacred. Cohen was no religious tourist. Rather, the singer “spoke multiple religions” fluently, always from his Jewish roots. At this 10th yahrzeit of his passing, it’s worth considering to whom (besides his audiences) he addressed his final performances. In “Traveling Light,” from You Want it Darker , he sang: “But if the road leads back to you, Must I forget the things I knew …Traveling light, like we used to do.” Grappling with God Like the ultimate Psalmist, King David, dethroned and on the run , Cohen was at a low point in his career when he wrote Book of Mercy . In those dark days of seeming failure, before Jennifer Warnes’s Famous Blue Raincoat revived his career, Book of Mercy was the middle-aged Jewish poet’s attempt to leave at least something of permanence: “We talk in this manner, we sing the time-honoured songs, and we compose new ones, as we were commanded,” he wrote in “25.” Yet, for me, it is Cohen’s final albums 20 and 30 years later, as his life neared its end, that most resemble the Psalms in how they grapple with God. Psalms for every human experience Through the years, Cohen addressed God right before our eyes in the person of a lover. At the end of his life, he boldly exposed the relationship that had been there all along — perhaps most notably in the song “You Want it Darker.” Here, he addressed God as “My lord,” incorporated elements of the Jewish mourners’ prayer and adapted Rosh Hashanah liturgy . Was Cohen writing and adapting Kaddish for his own impending death? I believe so, although in true Cohen fashion his words also mourn humanity overall, and challenge the divine. Leonard Cohen’s ‘You Want it Darker.’ As I wrote in Prophets of Love , for Leonard as “Cohen” (Hebrew for priest), existential longing and divine connection are inseparably linked at the base of the human condition. So, 10 years later, even if you are already a devotee, have a listen again. Pay special attention to how Cohen challenges, pleads with, chastises and even woos the divine. If you are not yet a fan, buy one of the iconic Canadian’s final albums, when he could feel death waiting at the door . You may find that, just as for many faithful opening the ancient psalms, there’s material in Cohen’s contemporary psalms for every human experience, including yours. Matthew Robert Anderson's research has received funding from the Federation for the Humanities and the Social Sciences (FHSS)

articles.content: Some of the world’s most powerful technology executives are investing heavily in artificial intelligence while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that it could threaten humanity. From underground bunkers to isolated islands , some of the industry’s wealthiest figures appear to be making plans to shield themselves from the very risks associated with the technologies that their industry is helping to develop . The benefits of technological innovation are not necessarily shared by everyone, nor are its risks. Those who profit most from developing new technologies may not be the same people who bear the consequences when things go wrong. Sociologists have long studied this unequal relationship through the concept of “risk positions.” Just as people occupy different positions in society according to wealth and economic power, they also occupy different positions when it comes to risk . At one end of the spectrum are those who reap substantial benefits from producing risks while avoiding most of their consequences. At the other are those who benefit little from these activities but bear a disproportionate share of the costs . Who benefits and who pays? The economic rewards associated with producing risks can be enormous. Industries that generate environmental damage or financial instability , for example, can create substantial private wealth while imposing significant costs on society. Yet few industries have produced fortunes as extraordinary as the technology sector. Some of the fastest-growing companies in history have emerged from the tech sector, while their founders have accumulated astronomical levels of wealth . The prospect of accumulating even greater wealth creates a powerful incentive to keep developing risky technologies . But this is only half the story. To understand why risks may be produced beyond what is socially desirable, we also need to consider who pays for them. When those who produce risks do not bear their full costs, they have an economic incentive to keep producing them, even when the consequences for society are potentially devastating. The more effectively producers of risk can avoid these consequences, the greater the burden placed on everyone else. In this framework, it’s not enough for producers of risk to benefit from said risks; they also need to be able to avoid any potentially catastrophic consequences. They need to occupy the positions of “value skimmers” — those who benefit from upside of risk-taking while avoiding its potentially devastating downside. They are distinct from “value surfers” who gain from risks, but also bear the consequences when those risks materialize . Preparing to escape the consequences The distinction becomes particularly revealing when considering the growing tendency among tech executives to prepare for potential future catastrophes . Several prominent figures in the AI industry have publicly warned that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity . Yet those warnings don’t seem to have slowed the development of AI at all . Locked in a battle for AI supremacy, there doesn’t appear to be an inch to give between competing tech giants . There are also concerns about generative AI that have come from within the industry itself. Employees and researchers working in the field have raised alarms about the scale and ambition of AI development, including comparisons to the Manhattan Project and technologies reminiscent of the fictional Terminators . Yet while some of the industry’s leaders appear to be doing their best to insulate themselves from these risks , their companies’ business models depend on expanding digital infrastructure and collecting as much data as possible. This expansion forces ordinary people to be constantly dependent on digital connection and leaves them fewer opportunities to avoid the risks associated. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into digital networks, those networks also become more vulnerable and risky. To prevent any aspect of our life from being outside internet dependence is to force us to be constantly at the mercy of technology companies. Could the public push back? German sociologist Ulrich Beck argued that modern society is one in which we must constantly face the social, political and economic problems of distributing a “poisoned cake.” His metaphor captured a central problem of what he called the “risk society” — the benefits of modern development are distributed unequally, while the dangers it creates can extend far beyond those who produce them. Yet Beck did not believe citizens would take this lying down. He argued they would come to see the reality of the risks being produced and act collectively to arrest control of this system away from those producing them. The conditions for such a moment may now be emerging. Protests against the expansion of data centres alongside parents’ demands that governments protect children from the harms of social media are just two trends that suggest people are coming to recognize their real risk positions. Perhaps people’s acceptance of bearing the brunt of the risks that they did not create is coming to an end. Whether it’s the people, the politicians or the tech giants who will win this debate is still to be decided. articles.description: Some of the world’s most powerful technology executives are investing heavily in artificial intelligence while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that it could threaten humanity. From underground bunkers to isolated islands , some of the industry’s wealthiest figures appear to be making plans to shield themselves from the very risks associated with the technologies that their industry is helping to develop . The benefits of technological innovation are not necessarily shared by everyone, nor are its risks. Those who profit most from developing new technologies may not be the same people who bear the consequences when things go wrong. Sociologists have long studied this unequal relationship through the concept of “risk positions.” Just as people occupy different positions in society according to wealth and economic power, they also occupy different positions when it comes to risk . At one end of the spectrum are those who reap substantial benefits from producing risks while avoiding most of their consequences. At the other are those who benefit little from these activities but bear a disproportionate share of the costs . Who benefits and who pays? The economic rewards associated with producing risks can be enormous. Industries that generate environmental damage or financial instability , for example, can create substantial private wealth while imposing significant costs on society. Yet few industries have produced fortunes as extraordinary as the technology sector. Some of the fastest-growing companies in history have emerged from the tech sector, while their founders have accumulated astronomical levels of wealth . The prospect of accumulating even greater wealth creates a powerful incentive to keep developing risky technologies . But this is only half the story. To understand why risks may be produced beyond what is socially desirable, we also need to consider who pays for them. When those who produce risks do not bear their full costs, they have an economic incentive to keep producing them, even when the consequences for society are potentially devastating. The more effectively producers of risk can avoid these consequences, the greater the burden placed on everyone else. In this framework, it’s not enough for producers of risk to benefit from said risks; they also need to be able to avoid any potentially catastrophic consequences. They need to occupy the positions of “value skimmers” — those who benefit from upside of risk-taking while avoiding its potentially devastating downside. They are distinct from “value surfers” who gain from risks, but also bear the consequences when those risks materialize . Preparing to escape the consequences The distinction becomes particularly revealing when considering the growing tendency among tech executives to prepare for potential future catastrophes . Several prominent figures in the AI industry have publicly warned that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity . Yet those warnings don’t seem to have slowed the development of AI at all . Locked in a battle for AI supremacy, there doesn’t appear to be an inch to give between competing tech giants . There are also concerns about generative AI that have come from within the industry itself. Employees and researchers working in the field have raised alarms about the scale and ambition of AI development, including comparisons to the Manhattan Project and technologies reminiscent of the fictional Terminators . Yet while some of the industry’s leaders appear to be doing their best to insulate themselves from these risks , their companies’ business models depend on expanding digital infrastructure and collecting as much data as possible. This expansion forces ordinary people to be constantly dependent on digital connection and leaves them fewer opportunities to avoid the risks associated. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into digital networks, those networks also become more vulnerable and risky. To prevent any aspect of our life from being outside internet dependence is to force us to be constantly at the mercy of technology companies. Could the public push back? German sociologist Ulrich Beck argued that modern society is one in which we must constantly face the social, political and economic problems of distributing a “poisoned cake.” His metaphor captured a central problem of what he called the “risk society” — the benefits of modern development are distributed unequally, while the dangers it creates can extend far beyond those who produce them. Yet Beck did not believe citizens would take this lying down. He argued they would come to see the reality of the risks being produced and act collectively to arrest control of this system away from those producing them. The conditions for such a moment may now be emerging. Protests against the expansion of data centres alongside parents’ demands that governments protect children from the harms of social media are just two trends that suggest people are coming to recognize their real risk positions. Perhaps people’s acceptance of bearing the brunt of the risks that they did not create is coming to an end. Whether it’s the people, the politicians or the tech giants who will win this debate is still to be decided. articles.content: When a human picks up a coffee cup, we use predictive processing based on our understanding of the world. For a robot, picking up a cup requires extensive training and simulation. (Unsplash) Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems. The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration , creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking. AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes. “World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does. Read more: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking A falling cup, a complex prediction Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly. For humans, grabbing a cup like this is routine. Yet this simple action relies on the complex ability to anticipate what might happen next. Our minds constantly try to stay one step ahead by understanding events and their causes. We can foresee the mess that would result from moving an overfilled cup or imagine a sofa getting stuck in a doorway even before we buy it. These predictions draw on expectations that form when we interact with the world . What we anticipate can, in turn, impact how we perceive the world and how we act. One influential family of theories, known as predictive processing , proposes that perception works partly in this way. The brain generates expectations, compares them to the information it receives and makes adjustments when the two don’t match. Let’s return to the example of the cup. Imagine reaching for an empty cup that you believe to be full. Your hand, expecting a heavier object, lifts it with more force than necessary. The cup rises abruptly and feels almost weightless. That mismatch provides feedback that helps correct the movement and update your estimate of its weight. What we anticipate shapes our actions, and what happens next updates our expectations. All this happens just to pick up a cup. Does AI predict differently? Even for today’s robots, reliably manipulating cups can require extensive training and simulation . The challenge involves learning how the physical world behaves and predicting the consequences of an action. Chatbots using large language models also make predictions, but of a different kind. They learn to predict the next word or fragment of text . This apparently simple way of predicting can nevertheless produce remarkably capable systems able to solve complex problems. Take the sentence: “A hand bumps a cup near the edge of a table. The cup…” Having learned patterns from enormous amounts of data, a chatbot might continue with “tips over the edge and falls to the floor.” It can do so by predicting patterns from a dataset and without ever physically handling a cup. However, being able to describe plausible outcomes does not necessarily mean a chatbot has learned why they happen . Teaching a robot to anticipate This is where world models kick in — a broad family of AI approaches that aim to predict how situations evolve and, in some cases, how actions may change them. These models can learn from videos, simulations or recordings of what robots see and do. For a domestic robot, this could mean anticipating that gripping too tightly might break the cup, or that a wrong movement could tip it over. By incorporating actions, motion and sensory information , preliminary research shows these systems can help connect predictions with what happens in the physical world. A world model could eventually make the same predictions we do about a cup. And as it learns from actions and sensory feedback, the resemblance to us may become increasingly hard to ignore. Still, arriving at the same prediction does not tell us what knowledge supports it or how that knowledge was acquired. Same prediction, same cognition? To us, a cup is not only a cylinder on a table. It can be graspable, breakable, yours, mine, too hot or almost falling. Our understanding connects the cup’s physical properties to a network of possible actions and consequences. Predicting that the cup will fall reveals only a small part of that understanding. And this understanding develops quite early. Studies suggest that infants just a few months old already have basic expectations about how physical objects behave . Child-development researcher Jean Piaget proposed that children build knowledge through acting on the world. As this knowledge develops, they become able to mentally anticipate consequences without having to carry out each action. For humans, learning involves more than accumulating information about cups. It involves connecting experiences when reaching for one, feeling its weight, seeing it spill and eventually imagining what might happen without even having to try it. Using world models, AI can also learn from actions and sensory feedback, in addition to videos, simulations and other data. Like humans, they can learn to interact with the world. The question is how their experiences contribute to the knowledge they build and use. AI could definitely come closer to anticipating what might happen and using that prediction to act. This alone, however, does not show that AI perceives, learns or understands the world as we do. As AI gets better at replicating the results of human cognition, distinguishing performance from process will only become more important. articles.content: For some, the lesson in needing to look presentable to society began with a reprimand about scuffed shoes. For others, it was a warning about stray hairs, an untidy hairline, trousers that needed pressing or a last-minute stain. A parent was often ready to send you back to the mirror, unwilling to let you leave looking as though nobody at home had taken the time to care for you. Behind these admonitions was an uneasy mixture of affection and discipline. Taking pride in one’s appearance communicated dignity , but it also reflected the demands of respectability in a world where Black people have often worked exceptionally hard for recognition routinely afforded to others. No one needed to grow up attending church to appreciate the ethic of “ Sunday Best .” Rooted in traditions of dressing for worship, the practice reflects a collective belief that appearance can express reverence for an occasion and regard for those with whom we share it. ‘Sunday Best’ exhibition at the AGO At the opening of the Art Gallery of Ontario’s “Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style,” the crowd understood the assignment. Attendees arrived dressed to impress, bringing sartorial flair to the celebration. Conceived and curated by a transnational team, including AGO curator Julie Crooks and fashion historian Jason Cyrus, with Amanda Bock and Clare Sauro , “Sunday Best” brings together garments, photographs and personal effects spanning Black diasporic life from the 1880s to the present. Displays of church fashion recall generations of Black women and the splendour of dress for Sunday worship. Elsewhere, the distinctive uniforms of the Black Panther Party are on display, a nod to the role clothing and fashion play in political organizing. The exhibition also honours Black dandies , alongside those who have challenged conventions of gender through the way they dress. Among them are Toronto-based trans soul singer Jackie Shane and the late fashion icon André Leon Talley, a long-time editor at Vogue magazine , whose styles helped to expand the possibilities of Black self-presentation. The exhibition also contains references to ballroom culture that show how Black traditions of dress and performance have been inherited and reimagined for self-expression and communal recognition. Renewed attention on Black fashion The exhibition traces how Black styles and cultural practices travel through migration. Visitors may recognize traces of traditions from their own families. A hat may evoke an auntie preparing for church, a family photograph the sober pride of relatives posing for a formal portrait . The curators bring these expressions of Black life together, drawing connections between diverse traditions. The exhibition arrives amid renewed public attention to Black fashion. Last year, New York’s Met Gala put Black dandyism on the global stage with its theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” “Sunday Best” contributes to this conversation by showcasing the communal rituals that give style meaning. The exhibition calls attention to the pressures under which Black people have fashioned themselves. Respectability and beauty In an iconic 1956 photograph, Gordon Parks depicts Joanne Thornton Wilson and her niece Shirley Anne Kirksey standing beneath a neon “Colored Entrance” sign outside a department store, in Mobile, Alabama . Their elegant and dignified dress contrasts with the indignity of segregation. For generations, dressing well could be understood as a defence against racial scrutiny or a means of improving one’s social standing . But no degree of sartorial excellence could guarantee protection from discrimination. The demands of respectability also placed constraints on those whose expressions of gender or sexuality challenged accepted conventions. Covers of Ebony magazine on display offer another perspective. As a Black-led publication, Ebony helped cultivate images of Black beauty and achievement in the United States that spoke to how Black communities understood themselves, free from the stereotypes and expectations of mainstream audiences. Across these histories, the attention given to one’s appearance carried meanings beyond the judgments of others. Dressing for worship could express reverence, just as a carefully chosen outfit might bring pleasure or communicate regard for others. The Sunday best tradition thus emerges as an ethic of dignity and care, fostered within Black communities even when those qualities went unrecognized by the wider society. Black queerness The exhibition’s treatment of Black queerness unsettles the presumed divide between church traditions and ballroom culture. Black churches have held complicated relationships with queer people , offering spaces for artistic expression alongside experiences of exclusion. Through these church communities, Black queer people have inherited styles and sensibilities they continue to reinvent. Consider drag performer Kennedy Davenport’s viral appearance on The Pit Stop . Reacting to another queen’s outfit, she sang: “Black stockings, white shoes, shouldn’t be allowed in the church.” Her playful critique drew on the rules of Black church fashion, finding humour in a set of esthetic rules passed down through generations. Black queer performers have also helped shape gospel music and traditions of Black religious life , including in spaces where their sexuality was not fully accepted. In “Sunday Best,” the proximity of church fashion to ballroom culture highlights how these traditions inform one another. Through inventive clothing and performance, ballroom turns resourcefulness into glamour, creating spaces where beauty and ambition earn recognition. Read more: Black style and resistance: The Met Gala, dandyism and blackface in Canada A ‘habit of care’ In the exhibition, everyday grooming tools share space with dresses and photographs. Hairbrushes evoke the private rituals behind a public appearance. Many of these belongings have survived for decades. In her book Ordinary Notes , writer and scholar Christina Sharpe describes regard as “a habit of care.” She says: “It is appreciation and esteem. It is the right of repair.” Her words invite us to consider the attention given to these belongings and the lives they represent. The curators extend this ethic of care to bring these histories together. From garments and paintings to archival photographs and moving images, their staging treats Black cultural expression as worthy of preservation and public appreciation. Behind the displays lies the painstaking labour of conservation, ensuring these materials will encountered by new generations. Black artists have long struggled for recognition in Canadian institutions, giving moments like these added weight. In 2019, the AGO hosted “The Feast” , marking 30 years since the groundbreaking exhibition “Black Wimmin: When and Where We Enter.” The gathering brought 100 Black women and gender-nonconforming artists and cultural workers into AGO’s Walker Court. At the opening of “Sunday Best,” the carefully dressed crowd offered another expression of this cultural legacy. Across the gallery, objects once worn with pride had been kept with care, their stories deserving of the same attention. Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario until Feb. 28, 2027.
