articles.content: Is that smoothie boosting your immune system or corporate profit? Research found over 96 per cent of immune-boosting content on Instagram to be from creators that sold or advertised products or services. (Unsplash) We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular “immune-boosting” ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help. Immune boosting is an online trend. Content producers share immune-boosting recipes — from smoothies to soups to poke bowls and pumpkin loaves . Nutrition books speak of “ super powered immunity ” while naturopathic clinics share immune-boosting “tips.” The “boosting” phrase has become so commonplace that it frequently appears in health content from reputable academic institutions . The COVID-19 pandemic — more so than ever in recent memory — had the public thinking hard about immunity . As interdisciplinary public health researchers studying the influential forces that shape public perceptions, the rise of immune-boosting discourse during this time caught our attention. We researched the trending concept in Google search results and on social media sites like Instagram . We found it to be problematic in two ways: First, content often presents scientific inaccuracies about how the immune system functions; second, it showcases corporations that push ineffective products or services. At a time when trust in evidence-based interventions like vaccines is on shaky ground , this can lead to negative outcomes for our health. Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Balance, don’t supercharge Not all immunity-boosting content is inaccurate or harmful. Information from research or medical organizations often focuses on healthy eating, exercising , getting proper sleep and avoiding the harms of tobacco and alcohol . The idea of boosting or enhancing one’s immunity, however, remains fundamentally flawed. The immune system needs maintaining, not enhancing. That’s because each person’s immune system is complex, made up of cells, tissues, organs and proteins. This system works innately and non-specifically to keep harmful invader germs out, using, for example, the skin and mucous membranes as a protective barrier. It also works adaptively, deploying a targeted and specific response for harmful invaders. The body’s primary immune response. (Wikimedia Commons/Sciencia58) , CC BY-SA The adaptive immune system uses B-cells that produce antibodies — special proteins that attach to invader germs and either mark them for destruction or neutralize their effects. There are also T-cells, which act as destroyers, hunting and killing cells that have been infected by germs . Amazingly, the adaptive process of the immune system builds memory cells of the pathogens it battles. When the same invader re-enters the body, it can be quickly recognized and targeted more effectively. A well-functioning immune system also correctly differentiates between your own cells versus invader cells . An under-performing immune system increases the possibility and severity of infection . But an over-active immune system can lead to a host of autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Maintaining the immune system therefore involves balance — not supercharging its functions and abilities. Corporations boost profits Those who promote the concept of “immune boosting” are often simply trying to generate profit. The very idea of “boosting” can create a sentiment of lacking — that one’s health could (always) be better. This frames health status as a deficit requiring people to continually pursue restorative or optimization efforts — a commonly used health and wellness marketing strategy . The first step is to establish a void, accompanied by anxiety or fear. The second step is to offer purchasable actions that address the void. Our research on Instagram during the pandemic, for example, found that more than 96 per cent of the immune-boosting content we reviewed came from creators that sold or advertised products or services. We found 62 different companies tagged in a sample of 28 posts. We also reflected on how the social media hashtag #immunebooster itself functioned as a rhetorical product used to “generate activity in the online attention economy .” Other companies may promote immunity-enhancing products or services with immunity-enhancing claims, such as hydrotherapy , IV drips, cleanses and detoxes . Cereal companies in the past have also marketed their products as “supporting” immunity . There is no good evidence that any of these activities have immune-function benefit. Stem-cell supplements Dietary supplements in the form of vitamins, minerals or herbs also offer limited benefit to those without diagnosed deficiencies. As noted in an immune-boosting article by a Canadian pharmaceutical chain, “to date, no drug, product or natural remedy has been officially approved by Health Canada to boost the immune system.” Yet corporations market them as either explicitly boosting or generally offering benefit to the immune system . Recent research from our team , for example, assessed the marketing of “stem cell” supplements on the e-commerce marketplace, Amazon. We found more than 40 per cent of the products claimed immunity-related benefits. Supplements are now big business, with a market valuation in the hundreds of billions . It is not surprising to find a broad, all-encompassing marketing approach to products such as “stem cell” supplements that have no clear evidence of efficacy for any health ailment Trust in medicine The commercialization of immunity is a concern for all of us. Commercialized health spaces , can damage trust in health-care systems and confusion around who and what we trust . If our perceptions are shaped by companies and influencers , this might negatively influence vital evidence-based health activities, such as vaccination. Rampant vaccine misinformation during the pandemic dissuaded vaccine uptake and helped promote inaccurate ideas of personal immunity . Vaccine hesitancy is highly complex, with multiple factors at play. Politics and polarization are increasingly influential forces . Inaccurate immunity discourse only further clouds information landscapes and, in turn, vaccination decision-making. Health and wellness marketing is savvy and alluring, carefully crafted to pique our interest and provide solutions. In today’s media environments, we all need to be cautious and critical of companies marketing products and services for our health and well-being. It matters when assessing preparedness for any future pandemic , and how our health-care systems can build and maintain public trust. Accurate understandings of immunity help us maintain well-functioning immune systems and a well-functioning society. articles.description: Is that smoothie boosting your immune system or corporate profit? Research found over 96 per cent of immune-boosting content on Instagram to be from creators that sold or advertised products or services. (Unsplash) We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular “immune-boosting” ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help. Immune boosting is an online trend. Content producers share immune-boosting recipes — from smoothies to soups to poke bowls and pumpkin loaves . Nutrition books speak of “ super powered immunity ” while naturopathic clinics share immune-boosting “tips.” The “boosting” phrase has become so commonplace that it frequently appears in health content from reputable academic institutions . The COVID-19 pandemic — more so than ever in recent memory — had the public thinking hard about immunity . As interdisciplinary public health researchers studying the influential forces that shape public perceptions, the rise of immune-boosting discourse during this time caught our attention. We researched the trending concept in Google search results and on social media sites like Instagram . We found it to be problematic in two ways: First, content often presents scientific inaccuracies about how the immune system functions; second, it showcases corporations that push ineffective products or services. At a time when trust in evidence-based interventions like vaccines is on shaky ground , this can lead to negative outcomes for our health. Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Balance, don’t supercharge Not all immunity-boosting content is inaccurate or harmful. Information from research or medical organizations often focuses on healthy eating, exercising , getting proper sleep and avoiding the harms of tobacco and alcohol . The idea of boosting or enhancing one’s immunity, however, remains fundamentally flawed. The immune system needs maintaining, not enhancing. That’s because each person’s immune system is complex, made up of cells, tissues, organs and proteins. This system works innately and non-specifically to keep harmful invader germs out, using, for example, the skin and mucous membranes as a protective barrier. It also works adaptively, deploying a targeted and specific response for harmful invaders. The body’s primary immune response. (Wikimedia Commons/Sciencia58) , CC BY-SA The adaptive immune system uses B-cells that produce antibodies — special proteins that attach to invader germs and either mark them for destruction or neutralize their effects. There are also T-cells, which act as destroyers, hunting and killing cells that have been infected by germs . Amazingly, the adaptive process of the immune system builds memory cells of the pathogens it battles. When the same invader re-enters the body, it can be quickly recognized and targeted more effectively. A well-functioning immune system also correctly differentiates between your own cells versus invader cells . An under-performing immune system increases the possibility and severity of infection . But an over-active immune system can lead to a host of autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Maintaining the immune system therefore involves balance — not supercharging its functions and abilities. Corporations boost profits Those who promote the concept of “immune boosting” are often simply trying to generate profit. The very idea of “boosting” can create a sentiment of lacking — that one’s health could (always) be better. This frames health status as a deficit requiring people to continually pursue restorative or optimization efforts — a commonly used health and wellness marketing strategy . The first step is to establish a void, accompanied by anxiety or fear. The second step is to offer purchasable actions that address the void. Our research on Instagram during the pandemic, for example, found that more than 96 per cent of the immune-boosting content we reviewed came from creators that sold or advertised products or services. We found 62 different companies tagged in a sample of 28 posts. We also reflected on how the social media hashtag #immunebooster itself functioned as a rhetorical product used to “generate activity in the online attention economy .” Other companies may promote immunity-enhancing products or services with immunity-enhancing claims, such as hydrotherapy , IV drips, cleanses and detoxes . Cereal companies in the past have also marketed their products as “supporting” immunity . There is no good evidence that any of these activities have immune-function benefit. Stem-cell supplements Dietary supplements in the form of vitamins, minerals or herbs also offer limited benefit to those without diagnosed deficiencies. As noted in an immune-boosting article by a Canadian pharmaceutical chain, “to date, no drug, product or natural remedy has been officially approved by Health Canada to boost the immune system.” Yet corporations market them as either explicitly boosting or generally offering benefit to the immune system . articles.content: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere — in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the “meno-boom,” and booms attract business. The Canadian menopause wellness market — meaning the products, treatments and services designed and sold to help women manage symptoms before, during and after menopause — is projected to reach a revenue of US$784.9 million by 2030 . But alongside the marketing are sensational claims and outright misinformation , including about how the menopausal transition affects mental health. That’s exactly what my research team has been studying for more than a decade. And as a woman now navigating perimenopause myself, I have a personal appreciation for why these conversations matter. I’m far from being in a minority: the Canadian Institutes of Health Research estimates that about 10 million people in Canada are currently navigating some stage of perimenopause, menopause or post-menopause transition . So let’s cut through the noise. Here’s what the evidence actually says about menopause and mental health. Before you know you’re in perimenopause The increased risk of depressive mood arises early in what researchers call the early menopause transition. This stage is marked by menstrual cycles that are consistently seven days shorter or longer relative to a woman’s usual cycle. Someone whose cycle used to average 30 days, for example, might start having 23- or 37-day cycles. So unless you’re tracking your cycle very closely, it can be easy to miss any connection between mid-life mood changes and perimenopause. It also doesn’t help that depressive symptoms have been shown to fluctuate considerably in perimenopause, making it a moving target. Not just about depression and mood swings Though a lot of research on the menopause transition has focused on depressed mood, there’s growing recognition that other psychological symptoms can show up too. For example, a recent study by our team , following perimenopausal women for three months, found that more than half struggled with moderate-to-severe anger and irritability. Weekly changes in sleep quality, hot flash severity, as well as hormones, predicted weekly changes in anger. Estrogen fluctuation in perimenopause has also been associated with greater sensitivity to interpersonal rejection , highlighting that psychological changes in the menopause transition can involve more than just feeling down. This fits with anecdotes from women that say they just “don’t feel like themselves.” Read more: Perimenopause usually begins in your 40s. How do you know if it has started? Hot flashes don’t explain everything Hot flashes are no fun, and they are extremely common in mid-life, with 60 to 80 per cent of women experiencing them in the years leading up to and following their last menstrual period. But as much as hot flashes may negatively impact quality of life, they don’t fully account for the increase in low mood that we see in perimenopause. For one thing, the timing doesn’t line up . Across the population, mood symptoms begin to increase well before hot flashes emerge. And by the time hot flashes reach their peak severity, depressive symptoms are already declining. At an individual level, this translates to many women experiencing depressive mood in the absence of hot flashes and many others experiencing hot flashes in the absence of mood changes. Hormone therapy isn’t a cure-all Menopausal hormone therapy is highly effective in treating hot flashes and night sweats. Vaginal estrogen cream is also a safe and effective treatment for vaginal dryness and sexual difficulties at any age. The benefits for cognitive difficulties (memory and thinking), sleep and low mood are less well-established. Multiple rigorous trials have confirmed that menopausal hormone therapy doesn’t prevent cognitive decline. And though it has been shown to improve sleep difficulties in women experiencing night sweats, evidence for its benefits in women without these symptoms is less conclusive. As for mood, the overall benefits of menopausal hormone therapy have been found to be quite modest, although some women may benefit more than others. Cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin-based antidepressants remain the first-line treatments for depressive symptoms, including during perimenopause. Future research may help us better pinpoint who stands to benefit most from hormone therapy. In the meantime, it’s worth keeping both its proven benefits and the limits of the current evidence in view. Not everyone struggles with the transition The increased attention paid to menopause and perimenopause is long overdue, and it stands to greatly improve mid-life care. Women should not have to suffer in silence or go untreated. But we should be mindful about how we discuss it. Women have long been dismissed as “hormonal” — meaning less logical, rational and level-headed than men. Careless narratives or conversations about menopause risk reinforcing that stereotype. Our research consistently finds enormous individual differences in how sensitive women are to the hormonal changes occurring in the menopause transition. For some, rapid shifts in hormone levels can trigger a host of negative mood symptoms. For others, the effects are negligible. Women experiencing difficult symptoms deserve recognition and effective treatment. But mid-life can also bring greater confidence, autonomy and opportunities for personal and professional growth. For some, menopause also means welcome freedom from menstruation and concerns about pregnancy. The “meno-boom” has brought perimenopause out of the shadows, and that’s worth celebrating. But attention isn’t the same as understanding. The research reveals that this period is more complicated (and more individual) than pop culture and business marketing can capture. Taking women’s mid-life mental health seriously means resisting easy answers. Jennifer L. Gordon receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR).

articles.content: The appeal of leading man Edward Ferrars, played by George MacKay, is ramped up in this version. (Focus Features) Director Georgia Oakley’s new, unfettered Sense and Sensibility delivers a contemporary take on Jane Austen’s first published novel. At the beginning of the book, Henry Dashwood’s death leaves his grieving wife and three daughters ousted from their home. Norland Park is inherited by the son of a prior marriage, John, while the Dashwood women relocate to a small cottage in another county. The novel focuses on the two eldest daughters, Elinor and Marianne (in Oakley’s adaptation, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles) and their contrasting philosophies of sense and sensibility. Oakley has said she was inspired by Austen’s emphasis on sisterhood, and some reviews have noted the film’s strong depiction of this . The director has spoken to her interpretation of Austen as a writer who “was taking what she knew to be a commercial form … the romance framework,” while including “subversive” content . The film seeks to translate Austen’s 1811 feminism to a modern audience, but, for me as an Austen scholar, some important things are lost. Bold women who revel in nature We expect Austen heroines to take long walks in the English countryside , but this adaptation, more than any before, firmly plants its women in nature. The film is beautiful to watch: In the opening sequence, Marianne reclines on the ground amid tall reeds and contemplates a caterpillar balancing on her fingertip. Later, we see her bathing her feet in a cold brook; Elinor skips stones with her love interest. This is Jane Austen, unbuttoned. Both heroines wave aside social decorum when needed. Oakley’s Elinor even makes the first move. Once Edward Ferrars is a free man, she boldly kisses him on the lips with a windswept landscape as background. In conversation with other adaptations Oakley’s adaptation stands in conversation with previous versions. As literary critic Linda Hutcheon argues, earlier adaptations may “ be just as important as contexts … as any ‘original .’” Oakley draws on Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation in some ways, including in the depiction of leading men. Austen’s Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon may be underwhelming romantic interests. But their failure to capture the readers’ imagination is part of the point. While Oakley does highlight the women’s relationships anchoring Austen’s novel, she presents the male suitors more favourably — and this undermines Austen’s subversion of the romance plot. Literary scholar Deborah Kaplan has argued that the 1995 Sense and Sensibility and the 1996 Emma “harlequinize” Austen’s novels. We might say the same is true, to some extent, of Oakley’s version. Trailer for ‘Sense and Sensibility.’ Fulfilment in romance? Lee’s 1995 Sense and Sensibility cast Hugh Grant and Alan Rickman, setting up their respective characters, Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon, as romantic leads. Oakley’s men in these roles, George MacKay and Herbert Nordrum, don’t (yet) have the same Hollywood star power. But they follow in Grant and Rickman’s footsteps in romantic appeal. The film suggests both heroines find fulfilment in the courtship plot that Austen interrogates. For example, Oakley’s Edward, like Lee’s, endears himself to the audience by playfully entertaining the 13-year-old Margaret. Such scenes don’t exist in the novel. Oakley further ramps up Edward’s merit. In Austen, it’s not a mark in his favour that he fell in love with Lucy Steele and formed a secret engagement. In Oakley’s film, the alliance was arranged. Once the Steeles lose their fortune, he is expected to dissolve the engagement, but Edward is a man of honour. Treatment of Brandon, Willoughby Oakley’s Colonel Brandon, like Lee’s, is set up as a romantic hero. I initially mistook Oakley’s Brandon for Willoughby because his first appearance — tall, handsome, moody — matches the novel’s description of Willoughby’s horseback arrival. In the new Sense and Sensibility , tension between Brandon and Marianne seems to be there from the beginning. As in Lee’s film, scenes are added to ensure that we trust Marianne has a happy ending. Herbert Nordrum as Colonel Brandon in dialogue with as Daisy Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne in Sense and Sensibility . Austen leaves us with less certainty. Near the novel’s end, Willoughby, having heard of Marianne’s illness, intrudes upon Elinor to inquire after her sister and offer an account of himself. It’s an explosive scene, and in the 1995 Sense and Sensibility , it was cut. Oakley keeps it — but makes significant changes. In the novel, Elinor is outraged by Willoughby, but she also pities him. As the narrator notes: “She felt that his influence over her mind was heightened by circumstances which ought not in reason to have weight; by that person of uncommon attraction, that open, affectionate, and lively manner … and by that still ardent love for Marianne.” Elinor can’t help but feel “a pang” for him. However, the film depicts Elinor as angry; he is a player, and she tells him as much, which drains the scene of its complexity. It’s curious that the film, at the same time, revises Willoughby’s villainy. In the novel, Willoughby impregnates a 16-year-old girl. In the film, his dalliance is with a widow of mature age. Loss of context around Norland Park The film, like the 1995 adaptation , circumvents an important backstory to the Dashwood women’s economic disenfranchisement. The Dashwood women are forced to leave Norland Park. (Focus Features) The novel’s opening paragraphs establish a complicated family history. Henry Dashwood, Elinor and Marianne’s father, inherited Norland Park from his uncle but on terms that didn’t let him leave it to them. Instead, the uncle’s will designated that Henry Dashwood, upon his own death, must pass the house to his son from a first marriage: John Dashwood, and, in turn John’s son, Harry. The narrator depicts this as unjust. The son already has an ample fortune. Rather than the proprietor uncle rewarding the Dashwood women for their care of him, he is swayed by the young Harry’s “attractions:” “an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise.” Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility , by contrast, doesn’t give this context and rather portrays the events as a matter of law. In this way, the film alleviates male family members from direct responsibility for the poverty of women. While there is much to enjoy in Oakley’s film, with its stunning cinematography and strong performances, it dilutes some aspects of Austen’s critique. Barbara K Seeber does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: People who visit emergency departments (EDs) but leave without their care completed are often assumed not to have been ill enough to require that care. However, the high rates of people who leave without completed care is a symptom of the mismatch between the Canadian promise of health care for all and the current capacity of the health-care system. The most profound effects of this mismatch fall on people who are structurally disadvantaged. Our research shows that the people who rely the most on EDs report the poorest care experiences, and often leave without their care completed. This creates a cycle of worsening health and increasing costs. Studying the care experiences of nearly 1,700 patients across three British Columbia EDs, our research team found that people facing the greatest social and economic disadvantages were more likely to report discrimination in the ED, lack access to primary care, depend on EDs for ongoing health problems and rate their care poorly . They were also the most frequent users of EDs. In a different analysis, our research also showed that EDs can significantly interrupt this cycle . Promoting equity Our team at EQUIP Health Care has been researching how to increase effectiveness by supporting health-care organizations to focus on people least well-served by the health-care system. In other words, researching ways to promote equity. Studying primary care clinics that serve people marginalized by poverty, racism and other forms of stigma and discrimination, we identified three key dimensions to doing so: trauma- and violence-informed care , cultural safety/antiracism and substance-use health. We also identified 10 implementation strategies. Our findings showed that patients who received care that promoted equity were more comfortable and confident in their care, leading to increased confidence in preventing and managing their health problems. This, in turn, improved their health outcomes , including depression and trauma symptoms, chronic pain and quality of life. We learned that although education and addressing biases were useful for many providers, inter-professional conversations were needed to develop policy and practices to address racism, stigma and discrimination. We learned that disruption was inevitable and necessary, and that policy change was as important as changes to health-care providers’ practice. More effective care Based on these lessons, we partnered with three B.C. EDs to design an intervention to support leaders and staff to deliver care more effectively. EDs are under immense and increasing pressure, evident in long waits for care and high levels of staff turnover and burnout , fostering a focus on optimizing short-term efficiency. However, the intervention was designed to align with the quintuple aim of health-care improvement , which optimizes effectiveness by enhancing: Patient experiences and outcomes Health-care provider well-being Health equity Service efficiency Health system efficiency Despite significant challenges related to COVID-19 and the worsening epidemic of overdoses and deaths related to the toxic drug supply, staff at two of the EDs mounted intervention strategies. Results showed encouraging trends in patients’ perceptions of the quality of their care and discrimination in the ED, but there were no significant changes in staff sick time. However, most importantly, there was a significant decrease in the percentage of patients who left without their care being completed at the site with the most robust intervention activities. This is crucial because patients who leave the ED before their care is complete often return when their health concerns are more urgent, resulting in significant harms to patients and costs to the health-care system. It’s also demoralizing for staff. We examined how to build on and strengthen these results. Staff and leaders were committed to focusing on those with greatest needs. However, other priorities — such as recruiting and orienting new staff, and responding to escalating crises such as violence against staff, the toxic unregulated drug supply, and COVID-19 — overshadowed their efforts and curtailed the staff and resources needed. Resources and recommendations We identified 10 recommendations for systematically improving care for those who need it most: Initiate interventions within care delivery organizations Conceptualize equity as foundational to health-care quality, not as an “add-on” “Hook” participation by linking equity to the organization’s most pressing “pain points” Seek commitment to effectiveness from leaders across all employment groups Commit sufficient resources to ensure representation from service-users and all employment groups and sufficient leadership and expertise Compose implementation teams of people from all levels and roles, including service-users Assign leadership responsibility to those with leadership roles at executive and clinical levels in alignment with their skills and responsibilities Tailor the intervention to align with the realities of the context Provide some level of education and opportunities for interprofessional dialogue for all Reconsider how time is used to support effectiveness and other elements of the quintuple aim, not efficiency alone To support these recommendations, we created The EQUIP Equity Action Kit , which includes step-by-step directions, assessment and evaluation tools, discussion tools, action tools, videos, animations. We have free on-line courses to support the Action Kit and tools to support the well-being of health-care providers as they face challenging workloads, high stress levels and violence daily. Some resources are available in both English and French. In addition to EDs, many resources have been tailored to other health-care settings such as primary care and cancer care. Colleen Varcoe works for the University of British Columbia, and PreVAIL (Preventing Violence and Inequity Across the Lifespan) a non-profit organization. I have received funding for the research reported in this article from the Canadian Institutes for Health Research and the Public Health Agency of Canada.
articles.description: People who visit emergency departments (EDs) but leave without their care completed are often assumed not to have been ill enough to require that care. However, the high rates of people who leave without completed care is a symptom of the mismatch between the Canadian promise of health care for all and the current capacity of the health-care system. The most profound effects of this mismatch fall on people who are structurally disadvantaged. Our research shows that the people who rely the most on EDs report the poorest care experiences, and often leave without their care completed. This creates a cycle of worsening health and increasing costs.
